Career planning and future readiness · Lesson 1

Find evidence about your strengths

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Factors Affecting Your Values; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
Optional reference · Explore Your Occupational Options

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Explore Your Occupational Options ↗
Core vocabulary
Something you want to explore or enjoy doing.
An ability demonstrated through an action, rather than only a claim.
Something that matters to you about how or where you work.
A specific observation or record that supports a claim.

Start here

What can an experience tell you about a possible career?

Jordan likes making things look clear. After seeing Jordan's school poster, a friend says, “You should become a graphic designer.” It is an idea worth exploring, but Jordan wants a better reason than a friend's opinion.

You will help Jordan turn experiences into useful evidence. Later you will prepare a strengths-and-goals card for Amina, using a different set of notes. You do not need paid work experience, a survey account or personal information to complete this lesson.

Work through Meet the situation, Learn the method, Follow a complete example, Practise with support, Check your understanding, Apply independently and Review and complete. Pause after the practice if you need a break; your entries save automatically. The time you need will depend on how much you revise. Practice is a place to try ideas. Amina's completed card is your final saved evidence.

Optional references and word help stay available beside this roadmap. Everything needed for the tasks is on this page.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Jordan's experience notebook

An experience note records what happened during a particular task. It is different from a reference letter or an interest survey: it supplies actions that a reader can examine. Jordan wrote the notes below after two school activities. All people and events in these notes are fictional.

Experience What needed doing What Jordan did What happened afterwards
School-event poster Two classmates could not find the time and location on the first draft. Jordan moved those details to a larger heading, reduced decorative text and asked the classmates to check the revision. Both classmates found the time and location without help.
Three-person science display Three parts of a display needed to be ready by Friday. Jordan asked each person what they could finish, made a shared checklist and arranged a Wednesday check-in. The group noticed a missing caption on Wednesday, finished it Thursday and had all three parts ready Friday.

Jordan's reflection note

“I enjoyed deciding which poster information people needed first. I liked changing the draft after feedback. On the display, I liked making the next step clear, but I found chasing missing work tiring. I would like work with a reasonably predictable schedule. I also want chances to improve an idea after feedback. My current career goal is to investigate work that combines visual problem solving and clear explanations. My life goal is to keep regular time for activities outside work.”

A career goal describes a direction for work or learning. A life goal describes something you want your wider life to support. They can influence each other without being identical.

Check the notebook. Which detail is observable evidence of Jordan's action?

Learn the method

Separate three kinds of clue

An interest is something that attracts your attention or that you enjoy doing. A skill is an ability used to carry out a task. A work value is something you want work to support, such as a predictable schedule, variety, helping people or time to improve your work. “I enjoy drawing” is an interest. “I rearranged information so two readers could find it” gives evidence of a skill. “I want regular hours” describes a value. None of these clues chooses an occupation on its own.

A person can enjoy an activity while needing practice. They can also perform a task well and dislike doing it repeatedly. Jordan's successful checklist suggests organization, while the reflection says repeated follow-up was tiring. Record both. Hiding a difficulty would make the career question less useful.

An interest or strengths inventory organizes a person's answers to a set of questions about themselves. Its results describe what the person reported; they do not independently prove a skill or assign a career. Imagine an inventory suggests “creative work” for Jordan. The poster notebook adds actual evidence, while the schedule preference adds a condition to investigate. If a suggested direction conflicts with experience, keep the conflict as a question rather than accepting the label. No inventory account or survey score is needed here.

Make the action visible

“Jordan is creative” is a claim: a statement you would like a reader to accept. Evidence is the information that supports it. Useful evidence names the setting, the person's action and an observable result. The result need not be an award. Two readers finding the information is a result because it shows what changed after the revision.

Be precise about whose action it was. Jordan arranged the check-in; the group finished its display. Writing “Jordan did every part” would give Jordan credit for actions the notebook does not report. You can explain a person's contribution to a team result without pretending they worked alone.

Build a cautious pathway idea

A transferable skill can be useful in more than one setting. Organizing information might matter in a poster, a set of instructions or a customer explanation. Transfer does not mean that someone already knows all the technical work in a new role. A school example provides a reason to investigate; it is not proof of professional expertise.

Use this sequence:

Recorded action → possible skill → limit of the evidence → question about work.

For example, “revised a poster after feedback” can support “some skill in making information clearer.” Its limit is one school task. A useful question is whether Jordan enjoys repeated revisions for other people's purposes. That question could change the plan; “Is design good?” is too broad to guide a comparison.

Connect the idea to a goal

A provisional goal is a goal you can revise as evidence develops. It might be “Compare two roles that use visual explanations” rather than “Choose my lifelong occupation today.” Keep a career goal and a life goal visible when deciding what to investigate. A role might use a skill but conflict with a strongly held work value.

Financial goals can shape the route too. Wanting to keep training costs within a stated budget is different from wanting the highest advertised wage. Later lessons will connect goals to complete cost records. Here you are learning to state the direction and values before assuming a particular occupation, income or training expense will fit.

Dated reference record — ALIS: The article Explore Your Occupational Options, read on September 28, 2026, encourages investigating several possibilities and asking about tasks, working conditions and preparation. In this lesson, that becomes a question you can answer from supplied notes; it is not a requirement to interview anyone or leave the course. Optional original.

Show a first-step hint

Optional hint — Where do I start? Find a verb in the action column: moved, asked, made or arranged. Write that action before choosing a skill label.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Factors Affecting Your Values

You have read Jordan’s notebook. Watch or read how family, friends and other influences can shape what matters to a person. Listen for the difference between a preference and something a person can demonstrate.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera against a plain blue background; the spoken examples carry the main point.

Your values are kind of like your inner cheerleader. They motivate you to do the things you care about. Your values represent what you think is most important in life. So let's take a closer look at that inner cheerleader. Now this is important. Why you ask? Because your values help shape all of your financial decisions. What material things are important to you? How much money will you need? And how will you earn that money? Your values affect these decisions. But what influences our values? Our family, teachers, and friends play a big role in determining our values. Movies, music, and culture can make an impact too. Your value set is made up of a number of factors. Let's picture a big value web. Everyone's will look different. This is a big web. These values influence your financial decisions. Do you want a budget for a gym membership? Own an electric bike or maybe a motorbike? Do you want a budget for basketball tickets? Or maybe you're a fan of the symphony?

FINLIT 101 · Factors Affecting Your Values · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Jordan wants a reasonably predictable work schedule. How should that note be used?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Follow a complete example

Turn the poster note into an evidence card

Connect the video to this task. Use the video’s distinction as you read: Jordan’s poster action supports a skill claim; the predictable-schedule preference helps frame a question about work.

First I identify the task: readers needed to find the time and location on a school-event poster. This context explains why the layout mattered. I then trace Jordan's action: moving the information, reducing decoration and asking for another check. Finally, I use the reported result: both readers found the details without help.

The skill claim should fit these actions. “Jordan has shown some skill in organizing visual information for an audience” is stronger than “Jordan is brilliant.” It is also narrower than “Jordan can manage any design project.” We have not seen Jordan work with a client's budget, professional software or a deadline outside school.

Completed poster card

“During a school poster task, Jordan enlarged the time and location and reduced decorative text after two classmates had trouble finding the details. Both readers could then locate the information without help. This suggests some skill in organizing visual information and responding to feedback. It is evidence from one school task, so it does not establish professional design expertise. Jordan could investigate visual communication work and ask how often the work involves revisions and unpredictable deadlines. This would test the career goal against Jordan's wish for regular time outside work.”

Notice that the card does not promise a particular occupation. It explains why a direction is worth exploring. “Jordan has always been an expert designer” would add a history and a level of expertise absent from the notebook. Replacing that sentence with a specific action makes the claim more credible.

Now you will use the same notebook, but the science-display experience rather than the poster.

FINLIT activity · Use a career suggestion as a question

From Career Planning Assignment, page 1. The original questions ask you to try self-assessment tools, list suggested careers and apply decision steps to a personal career choice.

For this course, use Jordan’s notebook instead of a personal survey. Identify an action suggesting an interest or skill, then a question that would help investigate a possible direction. A suggestion is a starting point, not proof of fit.

Use this distinction in the supported practice, then make Amina’s own strengths-and-goals card. Go to the practice fields.

The original opens in the course reader. Write in this lesson’s fields; buttons pictured in the original page are not active here.

Practise with support

Build the science-display card

Connect the video to this task. Keep the two kinds of evidence separate in your practice response: what the person did, and what the person wants work to support.

The person and their stated goals remain the same. The evidence changes to the three-person science display. Keep the relevant facts beside your fields: Jordan asked what each person could finish, made a checklist and arranged Wednesday's check-in. The group found a missing caption and completed the display by Friday. Jordan found repeated follow-up tiring.

First select the claim best supported by these facts: organized a shared task / completed every part alone / enjoys supervising people all day. Use Check my choice. “Organized a shared task” fits the checklist and check-in. “Completed every part alone” contradicts the group record. “Enjoys supervising people all day” ignores the reflection and extends one experience too far.

Write short notes in Action and result, Skill and limit and Next question linked to a value. Then use Compare your response with a model. You can open it before finishing if you need support.

Show a first-step hint

Optional hint: Describe the check-in before naming organization. Use Jordan's reaction to follow-up to make your question specific.

Your work saves automatically in this browser. Check the saving status before closing.

Compare your response with a model

Your current response

Model to compare


    

  • Action and result: Jordan made a shared checklist and held a Wednesday check-in. The group spotted the missing caption and completed all three parts by Friday.
    • 

  • Skill and limit: This suggests organization and coordination in a small group. It does not prove Jordan did all the work or enjoys managing people repeatedly.
    • 

  • Next question linked to a value: How much of a possible role involves organizing information, and how much involves chasing other people's work? Jordan wants useful feedback and a predictable schedule, so both the tasks and timing matter.
    • 



Your wording can differ. Check that your action comes from this case, your limit does not erase the useful evidence, and your question could distinguish between two kinds of work. Use Return to my response and revise the same fields; writing is not automatically graded.


Check your understanding
Choose an answer and use Check answer for each question. Read the explanation, then change your choice if useful.


Which statement describes a work value?
Which claim stays within the science-display evidence?
Why include the missing caption in an evidence note?
A learner enjoys an activity but dislikes its rushed timing. What should a card do?
What makes a skill transferable?
Which next question could most usefully change Jordan's plan?
Apply independently
Amina's strengths-and-goals card


Amina is considering work involving practical problem solving. These are new fictional documents; do not reuse Jordan's poster or checklist as Amina's experience.


Amina's experience notes






Situation
Amina's action
Result and reflection





A bicycle brake rubbed during a community workshop.
With the workshop leader present, Amina compared the wheel movement before and after an adjustment and explained the observed difference to a neighbour.
The wheel turned without rubbing during the workshop check. Amina enjoyed finding the cause but needed help selecting the tool.




A younger cousin was learning a board game.
Amina replaced a long explanation with one demonstration turn, then asked the cousin to explain the next move.
The cousin completed the next turn without help. Amina liked making the instructions clearer.





Amina's goal note: “I want to explore practical work where I solve problems and explain useful information. I value movement during the day and a predictable time to finish. I would like to develop my technical knowledge before taking responsibility for unfamiliar repairs.”


Two fictional role sketches for inquiry: A repair-shop assistant helps identify problems and explain service information; this sketch supplies no actual employer schedule or qualification rule. A recreation activity assistant demonstrates activities and helps participants use equipment; this sketch supplies no actual balance between desk duties and active work. These are possibilities to investigate, not offers or complete occupation profiles.


Create one strengths-and-goals card in the fields below. Use approximately 160–240 words across the fields; useful detail matters more than the count.


    

  • Two examples and what they suggest: Explain both actions and results, then identify a supported skill and a growth area.
    • 

  • Goals, values and two directions: State Amina's career direction and life preference; connect both role sketches to evidence.
    • 

  • A question that could change each direction: Ask one specific question for each role, showing why its answer matters.
    • 



Use Compare your response with a model whenever you wish. It does not complete the lesson.


Use the idea in this new case. For Amina, use her own action records and goal note. Movement during the day and a predictable finish are preferences to investigate, not qualifications.

Your current response
Supported model: “At the workshop, Amina compared wheel movement around an adjustment and explained the change. This suggests practical observation and explanation, with tool selection still a growth area. In the game, Amina demonstrated a turn and checked the cousin's understanding; the cousin then took a turn independently. That supports adapting an explanation. Amina wants practical problem-solving work and values movement with a predictable finish time. Repair-shop assistance could use observation and explanation, but the workshop example does not establish independent repair competence. Recreation assistance could use demonstrations, but the amount of active work remains unknown. For the repair route I would ask which duties are supervised at entry and what training is needed. For recreation assistance I would ask how much time is spent in activities compared with desk work and when shifts usually finish. Either answer could change which direction Amina investigates first.”


Another reasonable card may prioritize the roles differently. It must use Amina's supplied evidence and avoid inventing qualifications, hours or results. Revise your entries after comparing.

Career planning and future readiness · Lesson 3

Compare routes into a career

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Career Planning: decision steps; try the short case check
  5. Follow the video example or its written explanation
  6. Follow a complete example
  7. Practise with support
  8. Check your understanding
  9. Apply independently
  10. Review and complete
Optional reference · Explore School and Program Options

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Explore School and Program Options ↗
Core vocabulary
A sequence of preparation and decisions that can lead toward a direction.
Something that must be completed before a later course or step.
A formal record of a qualification, such as a certificate, diploma or degree.
A benefit you give up or a cost you accept when choosing an option.

Start here

Two ways forward can have different costs and conditions

Leah likes organizing equipment and explaining how to use it. She wants to explore technical support at community events. An employer-training route and a college route appear possible. Before choosing, Leah needs to know what each route actually leads to, what she must do first and which costs fit the available money.

You will compare fully supplied fictional routes. These invented programs are designed to practise the method; they are not Alberta admission rules or trade qualifications. All research for the required work happens in the records on this page. Your final product is a primary-and-backup route comparison for Owen, a different learner.

Follow Meet the situation, Learn the method, Follow a complete example, Practise with support, Check your understanding, Apply independently and Review and complete. Take a break after the cost comparison if useful. Allow time for calculations and explanations; there is no timer. Practice saves separately from the final route decision.

Meet the situation and read the documents

The destination comes first

A pathway is a sequence of learning and work steps. Two programs can concern similar equipment yet lead to different jobs or credentials. Leah therefore begins with a description of the work she wants to investigate.

Fictional Harbour Events role record — Event support assistant

“Assist a supervisor with equipment inventories, room diagrams and visitor instructions. Follow the venue's approved setup procedures. This role does not include electrical installation or independent repair work. For this practice recruitment, the employer will consider either completion of its four-month trainee route or the ten-month Event Support certificate described below. Selection is not guaranteed by either route. Applicants need clear communication, accurate checking and willingness to ask about unfamiliar work.”

Leah's preparation and constraints

Leah has completed the fictional school courses Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 1. She has organized equipment lists for a club and wants more practice explaining unfamiliar instructions. She can live at home throughout either route. She has $1,400 available for the listed training/travel costs and wants to enter the field within one year. Everyday living costs are unchanged between these examples and are outside the comparison.

Two fictional route records

These records use an invented local school, provider and employer. “Completed” means the course is already on Leah's fictional record; it does not promise real admission anywhere.

Field Route A: Harbour trainee route Route B: Bay College Event Support certificate
Duration Four months after selection Ten months after admission
Entry Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 1; employer selection required Communication 1 and Practical Mathematics 2
Preparation chain No additional school course in this case Mathematics 1 must be completed before Mathematics 2
Learning Supervised venue procedures, inventory and visitor instructions Venue planning, equipment records, visitor instructions and group projects
Completion record Employer training record Provider's Event Support certificate
Fees $300, once $1,600 tuition/fees, once
Required supplies $200, once $250, once
Travel $120 per month for four months $80 per month for ten months
Timing Next selection round: March 15; places not yet confirmed Application closes April 30; Mathematics 2 must be completed before the September start
What remains uncertain Selection and training-place availability; pay, if any, is not supplied Admission, a way to cover the cost gap and the school offering Mathematics 2 in time
Reading check: Why can these two routes be compared for the same first role?

Learn the method

Compare destinations before comparing prices

A credential is a record of a qualification, such as a certificate, diploma or degree. An employer training record describes learning recognized by that employer. Similar subject matter does not make them interchangeable. A short course about equipment does not automatically authorize work requiring a different qualification. The link between a route and a destination must be stated or verified.

In this case, the employer has supplied that link for one assistant role. It has not said the routes are identical or that either leads to every technical occupation. Leah should compare the routes for the stated purpose and keep their different learning and completion records visible.

Recognize different kinds of learning routes

The names below help you interpret a provider's offer. They describe different learning arrangements; a longer list of credentials does not automatically make one route the best fit.

Term What it means for a route comparison
Certificate A post-secondary credential commonly used for focused preparation for an occupation. Check the particular program: some certificates are for beginning learners, while others require an earlier diploma or degree.
Diploma A post-secondary credential preparing learners for a field or group of occupations. Its admission requirements, learning and completion requirements belong to the specific program.
Degree A credential from a degree program. A bachelor's degree includes theoretical or academic learning; advanced degrees build on earlier study. The word alone does not identify a particular occupation's entry requirements.
Apprenticeship A formal education route combining on-the-job learning with technical classroom training and required examinations. Check the specific trade's requirements and the qualification earned. Ordinary employer training is not automatically an apprenticeship.
Microcredential Recognition of a specific skill or competency after a brief learning program and assessment. There is no single fixed duration or assessment format. Check what is assessed and whether the intended employer or next program recognizes it.
Dual credit High-school programming connected with post-secondary or industry pathways. Offerings vary by school. Alberta distinguishes single-enrolled courses, which provide high-school credits, from dual-enrolled courses, whose credits appear on both high-school and post-secondary transcripts. Check the actual pathway and credit recognition; the name does not mean a whole diploma or degree has been completed.

Dated source record — checked September 28, 2026: Alberta's credential guide distinguishes program outcomes and admission requirements. ALIS explains that microcredentials assess focused skills and usually add to other learning. Alberta's dual-credit guidance distinguishes the two course arrangements above. These are category descriptions, not admission offers. Optional credential guide, optional microcredential explanation and optional dual-credit guidance.

For Leah, Route A is the employer training record described in the fictional document, not a registered apprenticeship. Route B is the fictional certificate described there. Neither record promises transfer credit, a microcredential or dual credit. Their stated connection to the assistant role is what makes this particular comparison possible.

Trace entry conditions back to today

A prerequisite must be completed before the next course or step. Route B's Mathematics 2 is not a label to copy onto a plan; Leah needs time to complete it after Mathematics 1. Her current strengths help explain why the direction interests her. Her growth area—explaining unfamiliar instructions—helps her inspect what each route teaches.

Think in a chain:

Current experience and courses → missing preparation → entry decision → route → possible work.

A career cluster can suggest related directions, but a cluster does not choose the school course for Leah. The actual route record supplies the requirement. This is why high-school planning belongs in a career comparison.

Compare complete cost categories

A one-time fee is paid once. A monthly travel cost repeats for each month in the stated route. To compare listed direct costs, multiply each recurring amount by its number of months, then add the one-time costs. Do not compare $120 with $80 and stop: four months and ten months produce different totals.

The resulting total has a boundary. Here it includes the listed fees, supplies and travel only. We cannot subtract trainee earnings because none are supplied. We also cannot claim the total includes every living expense. An estimate becomes useful when you state what it includes and avoid pretending unknown amounts are zero.

Make a primary route and a real backup

A primary route is the option you would investigate first under the current evidence. A backup route is a researched alternative with its own conditions. A backup is not simply “do something else.” It might become possible after another course, more saving or a changed start date.

Show the trade-off: the benefit you gain and what you give up. A shorter route may fit a deadline but depend on employer selection. A longer route may provide broader practice but exceed the available budget. A justified choice explains both.

Dated reference record: ALIS's Explore School and Program Options, read September 28, 2026, recommends beginning with the intended direction and investigating entry, timing, costs and alternative learning routes. Specific program information belongs with its provider. Our fictional records supply those facts here. Optional original.

Show a first-step hint

Optional hint: Start a cost line with “fee + supplies + (monthly travel × months).” Label the total “listed direct costs.”

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Career Planning: decision steps

Leah has two route records and a $1,400 limit. Watch or read the decision steps: define the decision, set criteria, compare options, decide and reassess. Use cost, preparation and timing as Leah’s criteria.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: two presenters speak against a plain blue background. The lesson below supplies the pathway table used for the actual comparison.

Number two, make good choices. Follow our super handy decision making guide. This will help you with any decision, but will also help you make the best career choice for you. Start by defining the decision you have to make. In this case, what career to plan for, then establish your criteria. That's what's important to you in a job. Next, identify the options of most interest to you, and then evaluate those options based on your criteria. Finally, make a decision. You can always reassess and change course as you go. But following these steps will help put your priorities in focus and make the best decision you can. Career tip number three, get out and volunteer.

FINLIT 101 · Career Planning: decision steps · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Which action follows the decision method for Leah?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Watch a worked decision

How to compare two pathways

This illustrated video uses Riley and a different pair of training routes. Follow how it compares entry, time, cost and uncertainty. When you return to Leah’s example, use Leah’s route records and figures; Riley’s costs are not additional charges in Leah’s case.

Read the lesson’s written equivalent

Compare two career routes by looking at the steps, not just the destination. Imagine Riley wants to explore electrical work. A career title does not tell Riley how to enter the field, what training is required, or how much time and money each route needs.

Riley draws two possible routes. One begins by investigating an apprenticeship and asking what a sponsoring employer would require. The other begins with a named training program. Both routes need current entry requirements, a credential or training outcome, and a person or source who can confirm the next step.

Here is a fictional first-pass comparison. Route A might need nine hundred dollars for tools and travel, with a possibility of wages while learning. Route B might need three thousand two hundred dollars for fees and materials and eighteen hundred dollars for travel. These are classroom figures, not actual Alberta fees. Route A depends on a suitable placement. Route B depends on admission and on whether the program counts toward later training.

Now make a decision that can change. A student who needs income soon may investigate Route A first, but should not assume a placement exists. A student who can travel may investigate Route B, but should confirm recognition and total cost. Keep a source and access date beside every requirement. Leave an honest question mark beside what is still unverified. A good career plan is a testable next step, not a promise about the future.

Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.

Follow a complete example

Investigate Leah's trainee route first

Connect the video to this task. Follow the FINLIT sequence in Leah’s example: identify the destination, total each route’s listed costs, check entry preparation and timing, then name the next check.

I first check the destination. The employer explicitly considers its trainee route for the assistant role. I then check Leah's current record: she has both listed school prerequisites. That makes investigation reasonable, but it does not mean she has been selected.

For costs, I keep one-time and recurring charges separate. Travel is $120 × 4 = $480. Adding $300 fees and $200 supplies gives $980 in listed direct costs. Against the $1,400 available, that leaves $420 for the stated comparison. I do not call this spare spending money for every purpose because other future needs are outside these records.

Completed Route A note: “I would investigate Route A first. Leah has its two stated school prerequisites, it takes four months and its listed direct costs are $300 + $200 + ($120 × 4) = $980. That is within the $1,400 available for these categories. It also includes supervised practice with visitor instructions, which relates to her growth area. The next decision is the March 15 selection round: a training place is not confirmed. I would keep Route B as a researched alternative while checking its extra course and cost.”

“Route A guarantees a paid technical career for $980” would add three unsupported ideas: selection, pay and access to broader technical work. The correct calculation does not make those claims true.

FINLIT activity · Use the decision questions with Leah’s records

From Decision Making — Key Steps Assignment, page 1. Questions 1–2 apply decision steps to education/training and career choices. Questions 3–4 use a trip and an event as further examples.

Use questions 1–2 with Leah: what is the decision, what criteria matter, and how does each route compare? The worked example supplies the cost, preparation and timing evidence. The trip and concert tasks are optional extensions and are not part of this lesson’s required work.

In the practice fields, explain how the changed condition affects the recommendation. Go to the practice fields.

The original opens in the course reader. Write in this lesson’s fields; buttons pictured in the original page are not active here.

Practise with support

Complete the other side of Leah's comparison

Connect the video to this task. When a condition changes in the practice case, reassess the affected criterion. Do not restart the comparison from a route’s name or reputation.

Use Route B and Leah's same $1,400 limit. Calculate travel and total listed direct costs. Then identify the course she still needs and explain what must change before B becomes a workable backup.

Enter Route B travel cost ($) and Route B listed total ($), then use Check my costs. Correct calculations receive “You multiplied all ten travel months and included both one-time costs.” A travel answer of $80 receives “That is one month; this route lasts ten months.” A total of $1,930 receives “You added only one month of travel.” Other errors receive “Rebuild the line: $1,600 + $250 + ($80 × 10).”

Write in Preparation still needed, Trade-off and funding gap and Backup condition and checkpoint. Short notes are enough.

Work-related experiences · Lesson 1

Show what you can do at work

Learning goal

Use a job advertisement and an applicant’s past experiences to write a truthful example of a skill.

What you will produce

A short application response for Rowan: one job duty and one or two sentences showing a matching experience.

How to complete this lessonRead, follow an example, practise, then write
  1. Meet Rowan. Read the situation so you know whose application you are preparing.
  2. Read the two documents. Learn what a job posting tells you, then read Rowan’s experience notes. Answer the short question about the posting.
  3. Learn how to show a skill. Read the claim-and-action comparison. Watch or read the FINLIT skills excerpt and try its short check. Then follow Rowan’s complete application example.
  4. Try the same method. In guided practice, check your evidence match, plan and write a response, then compare and revise.
  5. Check your understanding. Answer the six practice questions and read their explanations.
  6. Use a new case. In the festival application, use the new posting and notes to write your own response as Rowan.
Skills for SuccessOptional reference · Government of Canada

If you want another explanation of communication or collaboration, open the official skill descriptions and choose that heading. These descriptions name skills; Rowan’s actions will supply the evidence. Everything needed for this lesson is on this page.

Read the skill descriptions ↗
Core vocabulary
A notice describing a role, its duties and what an applicant is asked to provide.
Notes about what someone actually did in a particular situation.
Something a person did that can be described specifically.
What happened after the action, limited to what the record supports.

Start with the situation

Rowan is applying for a first job

Prairie Library Hub runs Saturday activities for families. It needs someone at the welcome desk to greet visitors, explain how to sign in and help keep its records accurate. Rowan would like this job but has never been paid to work in a library.

An application is a request to be considered for a job. In this lesson, the employer asks applicants for a short written example of relevant experience.

Rowan has helped at school and community events. Those experiences may show skills the library needs. The challenge is to choose a useful example and explain it honestly, instead of simply writing “I would be good at this job.”

Your role: help Rowan prepare a short application response. You will read the employer’s advertisement, find a matching experience in Rowan’s notes and write as Rowan using “I.” You do not need to supply your own work history.

First, find out what the employer needs. Then look at what Rowan has already done.

Read the employer’s advertisement

What is a job posting?

A job posting is an advertisement an employer uses to find someone for a job. It usually tells you the job title, the work involved, qualifications or skills, practical details such as hours, and how to apply. Its duties are the tasks the successful applicant would do.

At this hub, signing in means recording that you have arrived. Reservation records list the people who have booked a place in an activity.

Read this practice notice in two passes. First, use the title and hours to understand the role. Then read “What you will do.” Those duties tell Rowan which experiences would be useful in an application.

Prairie Library Hub · Community programs

We’re hiring a Welcome Desk Helper

Help families get a clear, friendly start to our Saturday activities.

When
Four-hour Saturday events
Where
Community program welcome desk
Getting started
Training provided

About the role

You will be one of the first people visitors meet. You will help them understand the sign-in process and ask a supervisor when a request is unfamiliar.

What you will do

  • Welcome visitors and explain the sign-in process.
  • Keep reservation records accurate.
  • Ask for help with unfamiliar requests.
  • Protect visitor information.

What we are looking for

Clear communication, careful organization, sound judgement and respect for privacy.

Tell us about your experience

Give a short example of something you have done that matches one of these duties. Your example may come from school, volunteering or a community activity.

Practice job notice created for this lesson. This is a fictional opening.

Find the work Rowan would do

Which detail tells Rowan what the helper would actually do?

The posting tells us what the library needs. It does not tell us whether Rowan can do it. For that, we need an example from Rowan’s past experience.

Read the applicant’s preparation notes

What has Rowan already done?

Before applying, Rowan made notes about three school and community activities. These are experience notes: a way to remember what happened and choose examples for an application. They are not an employer’s form or a list of job requirements.

For each activity, notice the situation, what Rowan did and what happened afterwards. You will use these details to support a claim about a skill. A paid job is not the only place someone can practise a skill.

Rowan’s application notebook

Experiences I can use in an application

School welcome evening

What needed doing?
Visitors needed to sign in. Two student helpers needed to know their roles at the table.
What did I do?
I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to the two helpers.
What happened?
The helpers followed the order and the table opened on time.

Club attendance list

What needed doing?
The club attendance list needed to match the permission forms.
What did I do?
I checked the names against the forms, found two missing forms and asked the staff adviser before changing the list.
What happened?
The adviser obtained the missing forms. I then updated the list with verified names.

Community event

What needed doing?
Families arriving at the event needed to find their activity rooms.
What did I do?
I greeted families, gave directions and checked that each person knew where to go.
What happened?
The families could identify where their activities were taking place.

Rowan has not worked at a library or managed confidential library records. Do not add either claim.

You now have both sides of the application: the employer’s duties and Rowan’s experiences. Next, learn how to connect them in a sentence the employer can understand.

Learn how to choose evidence

Show the action behind a skill

A skill is an ability someone uses to do a task. For example, explaining instructions is a communication skill. An employer cannot tell how Rowan communicates from the sentence “I am a good communicator.” That sentence makes a claim but gives no example.

A claim on its own

“I am organized.”

This names a quality. It does not explain what Rowan did or why an employer should believe the claim.

A claim supported by an action

“I created a three-step sign-in order and explained the roles to two helpers.”

The employer can picture the action and ask Rowan how it worked.

That specific example is evidence: information supporting a claim. It must also fit the duty. Explaining sign-in roles is relevant to explaining the library’s sign-in process. Checking an attendance list is more relevant to keeping reservation records accurate.

Use three parts to make the example clear

ContextExplain where you were and what needed doing. The employer was not there, so give enough background.
ActionSay what you personally did. Use verbs such as checked, explained, organized or asked.
ResultExplain what happened afterwards. Use an outcome supplied in the notes; do not invent a success.

A result does not have to be a number or an award. “The table opened on time” is a useful result because it tells the employer the preparation was completed when needed.

Describe the original setting accurately. A school example can show a skill that could be used at work, but it does not become library experience. If an example involves other people’s information, describe the task without including their names or private records.

The demonstration below uses the welcome-evening notes. Watch how the writer chooses one duty, selects the matching action and turns it into a short application response.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Employment Income: skills you can show

You have met Rowan and read the experience notes. Watch or read how communication, teamwork and initiative can be used at work. For each skill label, look back at an action in Rowan’s notebook that could support it.

Read the video transcript

So let's talk about the skills you need to get and keep a job. If you want to impress your boss, you'll need three types of skills. First, you'll need some kind of talent. La la la la la la. You develop your talent or skills through education, training, and experience. Then there are employability skills. These include communication, problem solving, positive attitude, adaptability, the ability to work with others. These are key to getting and keeping a job you love. Can you multitask, plan large projects, work well with others? You know you can. Finally, there's enterprise and skills. These are not only important to entrepreneurs. Everyone can benefit from having enterprise and skills. The ability to be creative, take initiative, try new things, lead a team, learn from mistakes, and find new solutions. With your talent and skills, you'll enter the job market. Here, you'll also need to understand the forces of supply and demand.

FINLIT 101 · Employment Income: skills you can show · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Which application line supports a communication skill with Rowan’s actual evidence?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Follow the writer’s decisions

Write Rowan’s first application example

Connect the video to this task. Notice how the example turns a skill label from the FINLIT clip into context, action and result. The reader can see what Rowan actually did.

We will answer the job notice’s request: “Give a short example of something you have done that matches one of these duties.” We are writing as Rowan, so the finished response uses “I.”

1. Choose one duty to answer

“Welcome visitors and explain the sign-in process.”

From the Prairie Library Hub notice

The useful action here is explain. The library needs someone who can make a process clear to other people. We need an example of Rowan explaining steps, not just an example of Rowan being at an event.

2. Find a matching action in the notes

“I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to the two helpers.”

From Rowan’s school welcome evening notes

This is a close match: both the job duty and Rowan’s action involve explaining a sign-in process. We also know the result—the helpers followed the order and the table opened on time. We can use those facts without guessing.

3. Build the response from the supplied facts

Context

At a school welcome evening…

Action

…I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to two helpers…

Result

…which helped the table open on time.

Finished application response

Duty: Explain the sign-in process.

“At a school welcome evening, I created a three-step sign-in order and explained each role to two helpers, which helped the table open on time.”

The context tells the employer where this happened. The action shows what Rowan contributed. The result explains why that contribution mattered. Together, the three parts give more useful information than “I am organized.”

4. Check that the claim stays truthful

Compare the finished response with “I am an expert at managing confidential library records.” The notes do not show expert status, a library job or responsibility for confidential records. That version adds facts Rowan cannot support.

The finished response names the school welcome evening and describes only the action and outcome recorded in Rowan’s notes. The employer can decide how that experience relates to the job.

You have seen one duty matched to one experience. Now use the same method for a different duty in the same library notice. The relevant details will be beside the task so you do not have to remember them.

FINLIT activity · Apply the résumé task to one truthful statement

From Tips for Preparing a Resume Assignment, page 1. The original assignment asks for a résumé for a hypothetical job and ten résumé principles from linked resources.

This lesson concentrates on the evidence inside an application. Use the supplied welcome-helper posting and Rowan’s notes to choose a relevant duty and write a supported statement. You do not need personal contact details or a complete résumé for this task.

Use the club attendance record in the supported practice. The final festival application uses the new fundraiser notes. Go to the practice fields.

The original opens in the course reader. Write in this lesson’s fields; buttons pictured in the original page are not active here.

Practise with support

Help Rowan show careful record keeping

Connect the video to this task. For careful record keeping, return to the club attendance entry. Choose the checking action and its verified result; a communication label alone will not answer this duty.

This time, you will support “Keep reservation records accurate.” Accurate means correct: the names on a list should agree with the information used to check them. You will choose an experience, plan the three parts and write one or two sentences as Rowan.

1. Choose the experience that fits

Which past action most clearly shows Rowan checking information before updating it? Read the choices, select one, then check your match.

2. Plan with the club attendance notes

The club attendance example is the strongest match because Rowan checked information before changing a record. Use the excerpt below to plan your response. Short notes are enough in these three fields.

Duty from the notice

Keep reservation records accurate.

Facts from Rowan’s notes

Rowan checked the club list against permission forms, found two forms missing and asked the adviser before changing the list. The adviser obtained the forms; Rowan then updated the list with verified names.

3. Write as Rowan

Turn your notes into one or two sentences. Use “I” for Rowan’s actions. Include enough context for an employer who has never heard about the club. Do not claim that the club task was a library job.

4. Compare, then revise

Open the model whenever you need help. Your wording can be different. Compare the facts and explanation rather than trying to copy every word. Your writing is not automatically graded.

Compare my response with the club attendance model

Your response

Your writing will appear here when you enter it above.

One supported response

“For a club attendance list, I checked names against permission forms and asked the adviser about two missing forms. After the forms were obtained, I updated the list with verified names.”

Context“For a club attendance list” identifies the original task. It does not claim library experience.
ActionChecking names and asking the adviser show care with records. The writer states what Rowan did, rather than only saying “I am careful.”
ResultThe list was updated with verified names after the forms were obtained. Asking the adviser is an action; the updated list is the outcome.

Use these questions to revise

  • Can a reader tell which list Rowan was checking?
  • Have I explained the check and the decision to ask before changing the list?
  • Have I included the verified update as the result?
  • Have I removed claims about paid library work or expertise?

Make any changes in your application response above. A different sentence is acceptable when it uses the same supplied facts and shows their connection to accurate records.

Quick check

Check what you understand

You have matched an experience and drafted a statement. Now check the ideas you used. Select an answer to see an explanation. You can change any answer after reading the feedback.

Apply independently

Use the method for a festival application

Rowan now wants to apply for a different opportunity: helping at a community festival. The employer needs teamwork and preparation. This case supplies a new job notice and a new experience from a school fundraiser.

Read both documents. Choose one festival duty and use the fundraiser experience to show it. Write as Rowan in one or two sentences, using the same context, action and result structure. You do not need to reuse the library examples.

Prairie Community Festival · Event helpers

Help our activity table run smoothly

Saturday community event · Training and a team leader provided

Your duties

  • Coordinate setup tasks with a small team.
  • Keep the supply table ready for visitors.

For your application

Describe a time you helped a team prepare for an event. Explain what you did and the result.

Fictional notice for this activity.

Rowan’s notes: school fundraiser

A new experience to use for this application

The situation
Three students had to prepare a supply table before the fundraiser opened.
Rowan’s actions
Rowan divided setup tasks among the students, checked which supplies were missing and moved extra materials to the table.
The result
The team finished setting up before the doors opened, with the needed supplies at the table.

Use the idea in this new case. Use the fundraiser notes for this new application. Select a festival duty, then demonstrate it with Rowan’s action and the result supplied here.

Before you finish

Read your response again. Check each statement when it describes your work.

Economic and financial decisions · Lesson 1

Read a pay stub

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Paycheque Deductions; try the short case check
  5. Follow the video example or its written explanation
  6. Follow a complete example
  7. Practise with support
  8. Check your understanding
  9. Apply independently
  10. Review and complete
Optional reference · Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Learn What Is on Your Pay Stub ↗
Core vocabulary
Earnings before deductions for the stated pay period.
An amount taken from gross pay under the statement's listed categories.
Gross pay minus the current deductions.
A total accumulated from the beginning of the year to the stated date.

Start here

Did the payment match the work?

Mika has received a pay stub: the employer's written breakdown of a payment for work. The amount deposited is smaller than hours multiplied by the hourly wage. That difference might be an explained deduction, an error, or a detail that needs checking. Looking only at the deposit cannot tell you which.

You will learn to follow the payment from hours to earnings to deductions to the amount received. Your final product is a short pay-check note for a different worker, including calculations and a question about a mismatch. All records are fictional. You will not enter your own employment or tax information.

How to complete this lesson

  1. In Read Mika's records, locate the period, hours and current amounts. Check your reading.
  2. In Follow the money, learn how the pay-stub parts fit together. Follow the complete calculation for Mika.
  3. In Check a missing shift, calculate from a second record, check the numbers and revise your explanation.
  4. Answer the six understanding questions, then complete Check Ellis's two records. Review the model and sign off on your final note before choosing Complete lesson.

You can pause after the guided calculation. All entries save; practice is separate from the final note. Optional CRA reference and vocabulary disclosures sit beside this roadmap.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Read Mika's records

Mika is an adult working at the fictional Pine Street Print Shop. A time record lists hours worked. A pay stub explains how an employer calculated a payment. A bank deposit is evidence of money received, but does not show the whole calculation. Read the two documents together.

Pine Street Print Shop — statement of earnings

Employee: Mika. Pay period: September 1–14, 2026. Payment date: September 18, 2026. Currency: Canadian dollars. This exercise includes one regular-pay line and three supplied deductions; no overtime, vacation-pay line, reimbursements or other adjustments.

Earnings Hours Rate per hour Current pay Year to date, including this pay
Regular work 12.50 $18.00 $225.00 $1,125.00
Deductions Current pay Year to date, including this pay
Income tax withheld $16.00 $80.00
Pension contribution $10.80 $54.00
Employment Insurance premium $3.60 $18.00
Total $30.40 $152.00

Payment summary: current gross $225.00; current deductions $30.40; current net deposit $194.60. Year-to-date net: $973.00.

Mika's time record: September 3, 4.00 hours; September 7, 4.50 hours; September 12, 4.00 hours. Mika confirms these are the hours actually worked. All deduction amounts are fictional supplied figures for reading practice, not rates or eligibility rules to use for a real worker.

Check your reading: Which two items should you compare first to check the hours on this payment?

Learn the method

Follow the money

Gross pay is earnings before deductions. For the single regular-pay line in this case, multiply hours by the hourly rate. The unit check helps: hours × dollars per hour produces dollars. The decimal 12.50 means twelve and a half hours; it does not mean twelve hours and fifty minutes.

A deduction is an amount removed from gross pay. Some payroll deductions contribute to public programs or tax withholding; others can relate to benefits or an agreed arrangement. The label tells you what is being withheld. It does not by itself prove the amount is correct or that it applies to every worker. In this lesson the amounts are supplied, so add them. Do not try to calculate current tax or contribution rates from memory.

Net pay is what remains after the listed deductions. It is the amount this statement says should be paid. Subtract deductions once: they are already removed from the displayed net amount. If you begin a spending plan with net pay and subtract them again, you make the available payment too small.

One-payment map: time entries → hours × rate → gross earnings → subtract current deductions → net payment. A second check compares that net figure with the actual deposit. A matching deposit can still come from incorrect hours, which is why checking only the last box is insufficient.

Choose the right column and date

A different stub may include several earnings lines. Overtime is pay recorded for hours treated as overtime under the applicable arrangement; an additional earning might be a separately listed bonus. Read each line's supplied hours, rate and amount before adding gross pay. Do not assume that every worker's overtime threshold or rate is the same.

A second format to read: a fictional adult worker's statement lists regular earnings, 10 hours at $20 = $200; approved overtime earnings, 2 hours at the expressly supplied $30 rate = $60; and a $15 bonus. Gross is $200 + $60 + $15 = $275. These are the statement's supplied terms, not a lesson about legal overtime eligibility. A separately labelled expense reimbursement is money repaid for an expense; inspect its treatment on the actual statement instead of automatically calling every deposit amount wages.

Current means this pay period. Year to date combines payments within the current calendar year. The figures serve different questions. Use current amounts to check this deposit; use the cumulative column to examine totals over the year. Never subtract cumulative deductions from one period's gross.

The pay period and payment date also answer different questions. The period tells you which work is included. The payment date tells you when the money is paid. A shift after September 14 would not automatically belong on this stub simply because payment arrived September 18.

Describe a mismatch without inventing its cause

If the time record and stub disagree, identify the two records, period and difference. An omitted shift is a possible explanation, but the documents may not tell you whether the cause was entry, approval or processing. A useful question requests a check of a specific line. “You stole my pay” is an unsupported conclusion from a mismatch alone.

CRA reading note — retrieved September 28, 2026: the CRA's pay-stub lesson distinguishes the pay period, current amounts and year-to-date totals. Use those labels to keep your calculation within one payment. Optional CRA explanation.

Show a first-step hint

Hint — First calculation: Add the three time entries before multiplying. Keep cents to two decimal places when recording money.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Paycheque Deductions

Keep Mika’s September statement in view. Watch or read the distinction between gross pay and net pay. Find those two lines on the statement, then identify the deductions that explain the difference.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a drawn pay slip separates gross pay and deductions and highlights income tax. The on-screen document is illustrative; use the fully labelled HTML pay statement below for the lesson arithmetic.

Often there can be a bit of shock when you look at your paycheck and see the gross pay amount, the amount before deductions, compared to the net pay amount, the amount of money you actually get. What is all that money that is being subtracted? Let's dig into paycheck deductions a little more so we can get a better understanding of what those amounts that are being deducted actually are. First, we have income tax. By law, an employer must deduct the amount of federal and provincial income tax you're likely to over the year and submit it to the government on your behalf. Taxes go towards things like roads, schools, parks and hospitals. You may also see Canada Pension Plan or CPP.

FINLIT 101 · Paycheque Deductions · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Which amount represents Mika’s current payment after the listed deductions?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Watch a worked decision

Read Mika’s fictional pay stub

This demonstration uses Mika’s May 1–14 statement. The current lesson uses September 1–14. Both examples deliberately use $225.00 gross, $30.40 deductions and $194.60 net. Follow the calculation here; use the September dates and time record in the lesson task.

Pause and decide: Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove?

Read the narrated and visual transcript

Slide 1: A smaller deposit

Start by finding the period—not by guessing at an error. Pay period • May 1–14; 12.5 regular hours × $18.00/hour; Gross earnings $225.00. What is the statement actually measuring?

Mika expected the weekend deposit to equal hours multiplied by the hourly rate, but the deposit is smaller. The first move is not to accuse anyone or assume every line is correct. Find the pay-period dates and the hours covered. This classroom pay stub is fictional; its dates, hours, dollar values, and deductions are invented. We are learning how to read and reconcile a statement, not estimating a real student’s tax or benefits.

Slide 2: Calculate the gross amount

Gross pay is before listed deductions. Regular hours 12.5; Hourly rate $18.00; 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00. Gross earnings = $225.00

Gross earnings are the starting amount before deductions. For this fictional hourly example, multiply 12.5 hours by $18 per hour. The units cancel: hours times dollars per hour gives dollars. Twelve times eighteen is 216, and half an hour at eighteen dollars is nine, so gross pay is $225. Compare that result with the printed gross line. It matches here, but the match cannot establish that the recorded 12.5 hours are the hours Mika actually worked.

Slide 3: Classify the listed lines

Add only the deductions shown as deductions. Income-tax withholding $16.00; CPP line $10.80; EI line $3.60. $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40

Now read the labels and determine which lines are deducted from this fictional cheque. Add the three listed amounts: sixteen dollars plus ten dollars and eighty cents plus three dollars and sixty cents. The total is thirty dollars and forty cents. In real payroll, eligibility, amounts, employer arrangements, and current rules depend on the situation. These invented figures are not current contribution rates, tax guidance, or evidence that a real deduction should apply.

Slide 4: Reconcile net pay

Subtract the deduction total once. Gross $225.00; Deductions − $30.40; Net $194.60. $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60

Net pay is gross pay minus the deductions taken from this payment. Subtract the total once: 225 dollars minus 30 dollars and 40 cents equals 194 dollars and 60 cents. The printed net amount matches. Do not subtract each deduction from the previous line and accidentally omit one. Also check whether the document has a different payment method, an adjustment, or an informational employer-paid amount before assuming that the net line equals the bank deposit.

Slide 5: Pause: try the calculation

Use the document, then explain the limit. Gross?; Total deductions?; Net? What is still unknown?. Pause and write your calculation before continuing.

Calculate gross pay and total deductions. What does a match establish—and what does it not prove? Pause to work it out.

Slide 6: Worked answer and next check

Arithmetic can reconcile while a record still needs checking. 12.5 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross; $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40; $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. Next check: same dates, actual hours, and applicable records.

The result is 225 dollars gross, 30 dollars and 40 cents in listed deductions, and 194 dollars and 60 cents net. A common misconception is that the deposit amount is gross pay; it is net in this example. Another is that matching arithmetic proves a pay statement is correct. It proves only that these lines add up. For a real discrepancy, compare the same pay dates with time records and the agreement, then ask payroll or check current official guidance. Never use this classroom example as a real deduction rate. Suppose the time record showed 11.5 hours instead of 12.5. At the fictional rate, gross would be 11.5 times 18 dollars, or 207 dollars, which is 18 dollars less than the printed 225. That difference is a question to check against the same dates and actual work record, not proof of intent. A clear follow-up would identify the exact pay period and ask payroll to review the hour entry. The invented deduction lines should not be scaled to estimate a real cheque.

Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.

Follow a complete example

Check Mika's payment

Connect the video to this task. Use FINLIT’s gross-to-net distinction, then take the additional step in this example: check the paid hours against Mika’s time record.

I start with the dates: all three time entries fall inside September 1–14. Their hours total 4.00 + 4.50 + 4.00 = 12.50 hours. That matches the regular-work line. I multiply 12.50 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross.

Next I add only the current deductions: $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40. Subtracting gives $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. The payment summary reports that amount. I can therefore say the supplied arithmetic and time entries agree; I have not independently verified real payroll rules.

Completed pay-check note: “For September 1–14, Mika recorded 12.50 hours. At $18.00 per hour, gross pay is $225.00. Current deductions total $30.40, leaving $194.60. These figures match the supplied statement. The record supports this calculation; it does not establish that the fictional deductions would apply to another worker.”

Compare phone contracts and subscriptions

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Smartphones and Plans; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently

Optional reference · The Wireless Code, simplified — CRTC

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open The Wireless Code, simplified — CRTC ↗
Core vocabulary
A temporary price that applies only for its stated period and conditions.
An agreement lasting for a specified period under its terms.
An agreement continuing by monthly periods under its stated cancellation terms.
An amount that the agreement says may be payable when ending it under specified conditions.

Start here

What happens after the promotional price ends?

Marin sees a phone offer advertised at $20 a month. The written offer also has a device payment and a later service price. You will read the whole schedule and compare it with using an existing phone.

Your final product is a recommendation for another fictional customer, with a full-year comparison and a shorter-use scenario. You will distinguish what the agreement actually says from what a headline suggests. No real signup, credit check or personal account is needed.

How to complete this lesson: Read Marin's phone offers and check the first bill. Learn Read the service, device and exit terms, then follow the twelve-month comparison. Try Leave after nine months, answer six questions, and complete Sacha's two service offers. Compare your reasoning, revise and use the four sign-offs. Pause after the practice if needed; your entries save.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Marin's phone offers

Marin needs at least 4 GB of data each month and calling/texting. The existing phone works, is compatible with both fictional networks and meets Marin's needs. Both offers have confirmed coverage for Marin's current location and include 8 GB, calling and texting. No extra usage occurs in the comparison. Marin can spend at most $45 each month after other commitments.

Offer A — new phone and service, twelve-month written agreement

Headline: “Service from $20/month.” Service is $20 monthly for months 1–3, then $38 monthly for months 4–12. A new device adds $15 each month for twelve months: $180 total, with no interest. No setup fee. All stated prices include taxes. Service prices are fixed to this schedule for the twelve-month agreement. If service ends early, the unpaid device balance becomes due immediately; no other cancellation charge is included in this fictional agreement. At the end of twelve months the device is paid off. Service continues at $38 monthly unless cancelled or changed under the stated process. No resale value is assumed.

Offer B — use the existing phone, month-to-month service

Service is $43 monthly; no device payment or setup fee. All stated prices include taxes. Cancel before the next monthly billing period without a cancellation fee; there is no partial-month refund in this fictional comparison. For the twelve-month calculation, assume this price remains unchanged. The notice does not promise that every future year will have the same price.

Check the first bill: Under A, what is the monthly bill in months 1–3?

Learn the method

Read the service, device and exit terms

A subscription is a recurring arrangement for access to a service. Its payment repeats until the agreement ends or changes. A fixed-term agreement has a specified commitment period; month-to-month describes a shorter recurring period. Neither phrase tells you every cancellation rule. Read the actual notice, payment dates and any separate device obligation.

A promotional price is a temporary price. Count the months it applies, then count the remaining months separately. Adding a device payment can change the bill even while the service price stays the same. Three labels are therefore useful: service, device and combined bill. The combined bill is the one that must fit the monthly allowance.

Payment timeline: A months 1–3 = service 20 + device 15; months 4–12 = service 38 + device 15; after month 12 = stated ongoing service, device paid off. B has one service payment and no new device in this case. This is a comparison of ways to meet a need, not a claim that buying a new phone and keeping an old one provide identical ownership benefits.

Count the whole period, then test the hardest month

A twelve-month total answers “What will the supplied plan cost over a year?” It does not answer “Can I meet every bill?” An average can hide higher later months. Check the largest required bill and the amount available then. Paying a low first bill is not evidence that the later schedule is affordable.

An exit cost is money due when the agreement ends. Some balances remain payable even when service stops. Here, ending A does not erase the unpaid device amount. Separate payments already made from the remaining balance; do not count the same device payment twice.

Use the right consumer reference

CRTC reference record — read September 28, 2026: the Wireless Code requires clear wireless contract information, including prices, service limits, commitment period, relevant cancellation terms and one-time costs. It applies to wireless service; it is not a rulebook for every streaming or gym subscription. Optional official page: sections A and B.

For an unfamiliar real agreement, use its permanent written copy to verify these terms. In this lesson all needed terms are supplied. No external page can fill a deliberately missing fictional price; flag the gap instead.
