Lending and debt · Lesson 1

Read a borrowing offer

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Why Borrow Money?; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
Optional reference · Credit: A 6-Letter Word for Debt

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Credit: A 6-Letter Word for Debt ↗
Core vocabulary
The amount borrowed or still owed before the interest for the period is added.
The charge for borrowing money under the agreement's rate and method.
An asset pledged as security for a debt.
A person who shares responsibility for a debt under the agreement.

Start here

A smaller payment can create a larger commitment

Two offers let Alex borrow $600. One advertises a smaller monthly payment but lasts twice as long and has a separate fee. You will identify what is borrowed, what is repaid and which facts an application would need.

Your final product is a borrowing decision for a different fictional adult, including a non-borrowing alternative. You will not apply for credit, supply identification or enter real financial details.

How to complete this lesson: Read Alex's two offer summaries. Learn Separate the money borrowed from the promise to repay, then follow offer A's complete calculation. Practise comparing B and an income change. Answer six questions and complete Bea's coat decision. Compare, revise and sign off. Pause after the product explanations if useful; entries save automatically.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Alex's two offer summaries

Alex is a fictional adult considering borrowing $600 for equipment needed next month. After all other commitments, Alex has $60 each month available for repayment and $20 separately available now for a setup fee. Both offers provide exactly $600; no optional insurance is included. All required payments are stated, and neither offer permits additional borrowing through the same agreement.

Offer A — fixed instalment loan

Receive $600. Repay $55 monthly for twelve months, starting one month after receiving the money. No setup fee or other charge if paid as scheduled. The payment total includes the loan principal and borrowing charges. Missed-payment consequences and early-payment terms are not supplied; they need checking before a real agreement.

Offer B — longer instalment loan

Receive $600. Pay a separate $15 setup fee from existing cash when the loan begins. Repay $31 monthly for twenty-four months, starting one month later. The payments include principal and borrowing charges; the separate setup fee is not included in the $31. No other charge if paid as scheduled. Missed-payment and early-payment terms remain unspecified.

Application-information card

A lender may examine identity, income, existing obligations and credit history before approving an application. A quote is not approval. Some products require collateral or another responsible borrower. You are reading a fictional offer, not deciding legal eligibility or completing an application.

Check the offer: What does B's $31 describe?

Learn the method

Separate the money borrowed from the promise to repay

Credit is an arrangement that permits borrowing. Debt is the amount owed after borrowing occurs. The principal is the borrowed amount before interest and other charges. Interest is a charge for using borrowed money, while a fee is another specified charge. Total repayment includes returning the principal; cost of borrowing is the amount paid above the principal, including relevant fees in the comparison.

An instalment loan provides an amount repaid through a stated series of payments. A line of credit permits borrowing up to a limit under its terms; repaid amounts may become available again, and the outstanding amount can change with new borrowing. A credit limit is not a gift or income. Paying only interest on an outstanding line-of-credit balance does not reduce the principal.

Offer-reading map: amount received → payment amount and frequency → number of payments → fees → total paid → amount above principal → fit with the repayment budget. Keep separately paid fees separate until adding the total, so they are not omitted or counted twice.

Recognize purposes and responsibilities

Different products serve different purposes. A vehicle loan finances a vehicle and may use that vehicle as collateral, an asset securing repayment. A mortgage is a loan used for a property purchase, with property security and further terms. A student loan supports education under its program's rules; it is different from a bank's student line of credit. A credit-card cash advance takes borrowed cash against credit, with its own fees and interest terms. Buy now, pay later spreads or defers a purchase payment and is still credit, even when presented as a checkout option.

A secured loan has specified collateral; an unsecured loan does not use a pledged asset in that way. Unsecured does not mean optional repayment. A co-borrower shares responsibility for the debt under the agreement. Asking another person to join an application is not simply asking for a reference; the responsibility must be understood.

An app can make a product convenient and can emphasize an attractive first payment. Ease of tapping “accept” is not evidence of affordability. Read the repayment schedule before treating the approval screen as a recommendation.

Test the commitment, not just approval

A lender's willingness to offer credit does not prove that repayment will leave enough for a particular person's goals and obligations. Compare the payment with available money and consider a lower-income period. If key charges or consequences are absent, name exactly what must be clarified. Do not invent a missing late fee, and do not silently treat it as zero.

Dated FCAC reference notes, read September 28, 2026: its line-of-credit explanation distinguishes a borrowing limit from money actually borrowed. Its buy-now-pay-later page identifies these arrangements as credit and directs attention to payment schedules and fees. Use these definitions to recognize the product before comparing it. Lines of credit · Buy now, pay later plans.

Show a first-step hint

Hint: Multiply the regular payment by its count first. Then add fees paid outside those payments and subtract the amount actually borrowed to find the extra cost.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Why Borrow Money?

The excerpt names reasons people borrow and emphasizes affordability. Alex’s two quotations let you test that idea with actual terms. Look for the difference between a smaller payment and a smaller total cost.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. No loan offer in the clip replaces the terms in the fictional document below.

It can actually be a very smart move for financially confident people. And there are different ways to borrow money. You can borrow from a friend or family member if you're comfortable with that. Many people also borrow from a bank, lines of credit, a credit card, a car loan, or a mortgage for a house. There's also some loans available from the government like student loans. Borrowing money can help you achieve financial and life goals. But it's important to borrow wisely, manage your debt well and limit your borrowing to what you can afford. You know your own financial situation best. So set your own debt limits. Don't let others set them for you.

The $55 payment fits the supplied $60 monthly allowance, leaving $5. That is a narrow margin, and the allowance is a planning assumption. It does not show how a reduction in income would be handled.

The payment fits Alex's current $60 allowance with $5 remaining each month. Before a real agreement, Alex would need the missing early-payment and missed-payment terms and a plan for a lower-income month. The quote itself does not establish approval.”

“$55 is cheap, so borrow” gives no duration or purpose. The complete note supplies a total and a limit before a recommendation.

Core vocabulary
Whether the payment and timing fit available resources and other commitments.
Credit that spreads or delays payment for a purchase under stated terms.
The point by which a payment or action must occur in the case.
An option whose availability and relevant conditions are supplied or verified.

Start here

Start with the need and the deadline

Credit can provide something before enough cash has been saved. It also commits future money. A useful decision begins with what is needed, when it is needed and what alternatives actually exist. You will compare a loan with a confirmed temporary solution and a saving plan.

Your final product is a short recommendation about getting required work boots before a supplied deadline. You will calculate the borrowing cost and test the timing of a cash alternative. You will not apply for credit or use personal information.

How to complete this lesson: Read Nico's device decision, learn Test purpose, timing and cost, and follow a comparison that uses a confirmed loaner. Try a changed deadline with support. Answer six checks, then solve Taylor's boots deadline. Compare, revise, sign off and complete. The worked comparison is a useful pause point; entries save automatically.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Nico's device decision

Nico is a fictional adult beginning a ten-month online certificate course. The course needs a device that meets its supplied technical requirements. This case does not claim those requirements belong to a real provider.

Device quotation: a suitable device costs $420, including all charges. A financing offer requires 18 monthly payments of $32, with the first due one month after purchase, plus a $20 setup fee paid today. No other fee applies if paid on time. The purchased device meets the requirements; its useful life is not guaranteed by the repayment term.

Nico's budget note: $100 is available today. After essential costs, $80 can be set aside at the end of each of the next four months. This amount is confirmed for the case. No later income is promised. Nico has no other device.

Equipment-library confirmation: “A suitable device is reserved for Nico from the course start until immediately after the fourth monthly saving deposit. There is no borrowing fee or deposit. It must be returned on that date. The same $420 purchase quotation is valid through that date.”

The equipment loaner and the money loan are different arrangements. The library lends an object to be returned; the financing offer lends purchasing power to be repaid in money.

Read the documents: Which fact makes saving during the first four months a possible way to meet the course's immediate device need?

Learn the method

Test purpose, timing and cost

First name the need, the job the purchase must do. Nico needs reliable access to a suitable device for the course. Owning it on day one is one possible way to meet that need, not the definition of the need itself. Separating access from ownership makes alternatives visible without dismissing the importance of the course.

Next mark the deadline. Money expected after a deadline cannot pay a bill due before it. Nico's fourth deposit arrives just before the loaner must be returned, and the quotation remains valid. Those details make the proposed sequence possible. If either were unknown, the plan would need verification rather than a confident promise.

Then calculate the whole obligation. Add every payment and separate fee, subtract the cash price to find the extra financing cost, and compare the duration with the intended use. Eighteen payments continue beyond a ten-month course. A useful purchase can still have costly or inconvenient terms; a label such as “education” does not settle affordability.

Separate a confirmed alternative from a hopeful one

“Use a loaner” is helpful only when its suitability, dates and cost are known. “Work more hours” is not confirmed income unless the case supplies approved hours and take-home money. A sound recommendation names what is available and what remains uncertain. It does not solve every gap by assuming a gift, refund or new job.

A loan application may request identity, income, existing debts and credit information. Approval is a lender's decision; the lesson's ability to calculate a payment is not approval. A co-borrower shares contractual obligations, rather than merely acting as a reference. Never add another person to a plan as if their consent and repayment ability were supplied.

Compare consequences across time

A payment that looks small can limit later choices. Conversely, delaying a genuinely necessary purchase without a workable alternative can interrupt learning or work. Compare the actual consequences of each feasible option. Use an explicit decision line: need → deadline → available alternatives → total and timing → recommendation.

Optional FCAC reading record: Buy now, pay later plans identifies instalment arrangements as credit with terms to inspect, including fees and payment timing. Read September 28, 2026. The supplied quotation controls this exercise; no real product application or outside reading is required.

Show a first-step hint

Hint: On paper or in the supplied note field, put “now,” “month four,” “month ten” and “month eighteen” on a line. Place access, saving and repayment beside the correct point before deciding.

Why Borrow Money? Repayment and alternatives

This excerpt contrasts paying a card balance in full with carrying debt and asks whether borrowing provides a worthwhile advantage. Nico’s financing is a fixed-payment offer, not a credit-card example. Apply the question about advantage to the confirmed loaner and saving alternative.

Read the video transcript

Getting into debt trouble can be very stressful. Stay on top of your finances. Live within your means and what you can afford. Set your own limits and use debt only when it's to your advantage. Now back to my pool.

FINLIT 101 · Why Borrow Money? Repayment and alternatives · selected excerpt, used with permission.

What allows Nico to compare financing with saving first?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Meet the device need without inventing money

Connect the video to this task. Apply the video’s question about the advantage of borrowing: does paying extra solve a problem that the confirmed loaner and cash plan cannot solve?

Financing costs 18 × $32 + $20 = $596. Compared with the $420 cash price, the extra cost is $176. Nico could pay the setup fee from the $100, but a first payment that fits today says little about all 18 future payments when only four months of available money are confirmed.

With the loaner, Nico retains the $100 and saves 4 × $80 = $320. The total reaches $420 at the fourth deposit. The loaner covers the time until then. This plan uses the specific confirmation, not a general assumption that equipment libraries always have stock.

Complete recommendation: “I recommend using the reserved loaner while setting aside $80 at each of the next four month-ends. With $100 already available, Nico reaches $420 before returning it and can use the valid cash quotation. Financing would total $596, $176 more, and continue for eight months beyond the course. I would confirm any changed loaner date or price before relying on this sequence.”

“Wait four months without a device” ignores the immediate learning need. “The $32 payment is cheap, so borrow” ignores total cost and the unconfirmed later budget. The model explains how access, not just money, is maintained.

FINLIT activity · Ask what the borrowing would solve

From Why Borrow Money Assignment, page 1. The original questions ask learners to research payday loans and lines of credit, including rates, access, uses and limits.

In supported practice, test whether the shorter loaner still bridges the time needed to save. Go to the practice fields.

The loaner is available for only two months

The correct cash amount is $100 + 2 × $80 = $260; the gap is $420 − $260 = $160. An answer of $420 includes deposits arriving after the new deadline. An answer of $160 as available cash confuses the gap with the balance. A zero gap assumes a resource that has not been supplied.

Saving, investing, and financial plans · Lesson 4

Check what your money will buy

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Investing Money: purchasing power; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
Optional reference · Inflation Calculator

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Inflation Calculator ↗
Core vocabulary
A rise in the general level of prices over time.
What an amount of money can buy at a particular price level.
The money amount stated without adjusting it for changes in purchasing power.
A money amount expressed at a comparison period's price level.

Start here

More dollars can still buy less

A balance can grow while prices grow faster. You will compare dollar amounts with purchasing power, then test the effect of a fee in a supplied calculator. The purpose is to understand a model and revise a goal, not predict the next year's inflation or investment return.

Your final product is an updated saving instruction after a fictional course-material price changes. You will calculate the new cost, find the gap and choose a feasible adjustment.

How to complete this lesson: Read A basket and a balance, learn Compare growth on the same time basis, and follow the purchasing-power example. Use the model to test a fee, then answer six checks. Complete Riley's materials target, compare, revise and sign off. The calculator has an equivalent supplied output record; no outside account or spreadsheet is required.

Meet the situation and read the documents

A basket and a balance

A fictional basket contains the same quantities of the same items at both dates. It costs $100 at the start of the year and $103 at the end. A separate $100 saving balance grows to $101 over that year, with no deposits, withdrawals, fees or tax in this illustration.

The basket is a teaching model, not Canada's actual Consumer Price Index (CPI). The 3% change is not a current inflation report. A single person's purchases can change differently from an economy-wide average.

Calculator assumptions: Starting amount $100; monthly deposit $0; period 1 year; annual effective growth 1%; annual fee 0%; annual inflation assumption 3%. The model applies a constant monthly equivalent growth rate and month-end deposits. It reports dollar balance and purchasing power in start-of-year dollars. Actual returns and prices need not follow constant rates.

Read the record: At year-end, can the $101 balance buy the unchanged $103 basket?

Learn the method

Compare growth on the same time basis

Inflation is an increase in the general level of prices over time. Purchasing power describes what money can buy. A particular price change is useful for a specific goal, but by itself does not measure all inflation. Bank of Canada's Understanding inflation explains this distinction through price-level and basket measures; read September 28, 2026.

The nominal balance is the number of dollars shown. A purchasing-power amount expresses those dollars relative to prices at a chosen starting date. In our model, the balance grows 1% while the basket grows 3%. The nominal number rises, but its ability to buy the original basket falls.

For a target price, a 3% increase means multiply the original amount by 1.03. For purchasing power after that increase, divide the later balance by 1.03. These operations answer different questions. $100 × 1.03 asks what the basket now costs; $101 ÷ 1.03 asks what the balance is worth in the earlier price scale.

Account for fees as well as growth

A quoted return before fees is not necessarily what remains for the investor. A fixed-dollar fee and a percentage fee can have different effects. You need the amount, base and timing. This calculator treats an annual percentage fee as one-twelfth of that percentage charged each month after growth and before any new deposit. Real products can use other conventions.

Do not simply subtract unrelated percentages without checking their timing. “4% growth minus 1% fee minus 3% inflation is exactly zero” is a useful rough intuition here, but not the exact model. The fee is applied throughout the year and inflation changes the price scale by multiplication. The tool makes the assumptions explicit so a small difference is explainable.

Use scenarios without turning them into promises

Appreciation means an asset rises in value; depreciation means it falls. A calculator's chosen growth rate is an input, not a forecast. Market values can move unevenly and may be negative. Fees, deposits and withdrawals also affect the final balance, so a balance change is not automatically an investment return.

When a goal's actual price changes, update the target using that specific information. You can revise the contribution, choose a confirmed suitable lower-cost alternative, or change a flexible deadline. Do not assume a riskier investment will produce exactly the missing amount by a fixed date.

Show a first-step hint

Hint: Label every number with its date: “price now,” “price later,” “balance later.” Compare price and balance at the same point before adjusting for purchasing power.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Investing Money: purchasing power

You have a $100 basket that later costs $103 and a $100 balance that grows to $101. Watch or read why rising dollar balances can still buy less when prices rise faster. Treat the clip as the explanation and the supplied basket as the calculation.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. The HTML basket and account comparison below contains the figures used in this lesson.

You need to protect your purchasing power of your savings against the effects of inflation. You see, as prices rise, each dollar is able to buy less. Makes sense right? If the dollars you have saved for the future don't increase in value by at least as much as inflation, the purchasing power of those savings will fall, which pretty much defeats the purpose of saving. Remember inflation? Inflation is the increase in the average level of prices in the economy.

FINLIT 101 · Investing Money: purchasing power · selected excerpt, used with permission.

What happened to the ability of the $101 balance to buy the original basket?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Follow a complete example

Explain $101 in the new price scale

Connect the video to this task. Follow the two measures separately: the dollar balance and what it can buy. This is the distinction illustrated in FINLIT’s explanation.

The basket rises by $103 − $100 = $3, or 3% of its starting cost. The balance rises by $1, or 1%. The $101 balance cannot buy the $103 basket; it needs another $2.

The calculator divides $101 by 1.03, producing $98.06 in start-of-year purchasing power after rounding. This is a comparison measure, not a withdrawal from the account. The account still contains $101.

Complete explanation: “The nominal balance increased from $100 to $101, but the unchanged basket now costs $103. The balance is $2 short of buying it. In the model's original price scale, $101 ÷ 1.03 is about $98.06, so purchasing power fell even though the dollar balance rose. The 3% is a scenario assumption, not a claim about current Canadian inflation.”

An answer that says “the bank took $2.94” confuses a price-adjusted comparison with a transaction. Nothing in the record says money was removed.

Practise with support

Test a fee in the same model

Connect the video to this task. In the fee comparison, hold the growth and inflation assumptions constant while testing the fee. Do not treat a calculator’s chosen return as a promise.

Choose Load fee comparison. Set starting amount $100, monthly deposit $0, years 1, annual effective growth 4%, annual fee 1%, inflation 3%. Predict whether a fee will leave more or less money than the same model without a fee, then select Calculate.

Supplied output record: With the fee, nominal balance $102.96, purchasing power $99.97. With fee changed to 0% and all other inputs unchanged, nominal balance $104.00, purchasing power $100.97. Outputs round at display only. The fee convention is stated above; these are not real product quotations.

Enter Displayed nominal difference caused by the fee ($) and select Which comparison is supported?: same gross return, lower retained balance with the fee, fee creates extra return, the two cases use different starting money, or the result predicts next year. Write What the tool helps me see, two sentences. Use Compare your response with a model.

The displayed difference is $104.00 − $102.96 = $1.04. If you enter exactly $1, you have treated the fee as a single charge on the original $100 instead of the supplied monthly convention. If you say the fee causes a $4 loss, you have confused gross growth with the difference between scenarios. The first comparison is supported; the others misstate a cost, a controlled input or the status of a scenario.

Your work saves automatically in this browser. Check the saving status before closing.

Compare your response with a model

Your current response

Model: “With the same starting money and 4% gross growth assumption, the fee reduces the displayed final balance by $1.04. The fee case ends at $102.96 but only $99.97 of start-of-year purchasing power under 3% inflation. The tool shows the combined effect of its stated assumptions, not a guaranteed return.”


For a simpler target check, a fictional $300 item rising by 4% costs $312. If $300 is saved, the gap is $12. Use this method in the independent task, then revise your fee explanation if necessary.

Alternatively, a suitable used set is confirmed available for $245, all-in, until the same deadline. Both sets meet the course requirement; the used set has cosmetic wear. No interest or market gain is assumed.


Enter New quoted price ($) and Gap compared with $248 saved ($). Choose add money for the new set or buy the confirmed used set. Write My updated plan for Riley, 3–4 sentences explaining the calculation, timing, remaining money and one tradeoff.





Use the idea in this new case. Riley’s task uses a confirmed new quotation, not a forecast of general inflation. Recalculate that specific price and choose a feasible way to cover it.

I would allocate $4 of the confirmed $10 next week, reaching $252 before the two-week deadline and leaving $6 of that new money unallocated. This keeps the new-set choice but gives up $7 compared with the $245 used option.”
Alternative model: “The new quotation is $252, $4 above current savings. I would choose the confirmed suitable used set for $245, leaving $3 of the $248 saved and keeping next week's $10 available. The tradeoff is accepting cosmetic wear; the case confirms it still meets the requirement.”
Neither plan needs an invented investment gain. Compare and revise your chosen plan.

Saving, investing, and financial plans · Lesson 6

Revise a plan when life changes

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read The Magic of Compounding; try the short case check
  5. Follow a complete example
  6. Practise with support
  7. Check your understanding
  8. Apply independently
  9. Review and complete
Optional reference · FCAC saving and investment goals

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open FCAC saving and investment goals ↗
Core vocabulary
A condition a plan relies on.
A difference between what was planned and what actually happened in the case.
A change or date that signals the plan should be checked.
A recalculated future result using the updated balance and stated conditions.

Start here

Keep the record; change the next action

A plan can be reasonable when written and still need revision after an unexpected cost. You will separate what has already happened from what can change next. The task is to recalculate from the actual balance, explain the adjustment and set a new review point.

Your final product is a revision note for a fictional saving plan after a necessary expense. It will show the current balance, remaining gap and feasible future contributions. No personal loss, income or account information is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's original plan and transaction record, learn Update from the present balance, and follow a revised contribution. Practise a flexible deadline and optionally test a monthly budget shock. Answer six checks. Complete Devon's changed plan, compare, revise and sign off. All entries save; the original record remains visible.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Ari's original plan and transaction record

Ari is fictional and wants $350 by the end of month 6 for a purchase. The plan began with $200, then scheduled $25 at each of six month-ends. No interest or fee applies. The deadline was initially treated as fixed.

What actually happened:

Event Change Balance
Start Opening $200 $200
End of month 1 Deposit $25 $225
End of month 2 Deposit $25 $250
Immediately after month 2 Necessary repair, withdrawal $80 $170

New budget information: Ari can normally save $30 in each remaining month after other costs. A confirmed temporary change can instead free up to $45 monthly for months 3–6, without missing essential costs or required payments. There is no other money available. The repair has already been paid and is not refundable in the case.

Read the record: Which balance should the revised plan start from immediately after the repair?

Learn the method

Update from the present balance

A revision changes a future action in response to evidence. It does not rewrite earlier transactions. Start with the actual balance, subtract it from the target and count the deposits still available before the deadline. This creates a new gap and a new required contribution.

For Ari, two months have passed. Only four month-end deposits remain before month six. Using six deposits in the revised calculation would pretend time already elapsed is still available. Similarly, restarting at the old $200 balance would erase both saving progress and the repair cost.

Change a constraint openly

There are several possible levers: contribution, target amount, deadline or a confirmed resource. Each has consequences. A higher contribution must fit the revised budget. A lower target must still meet the need. A later date must actually be flexible. A resource must be confirmed rather than hoped for.

Sometimes no combination satisfies every original condition. Naming the conflict is better planning than hiding it. A revision note should say which condition changes and why. It should also distinguish a temporary adjustment from an ongoing one so that next month's plan does not accidentally repeat a one-time cost.

Review goals as circumstances change

Education, work, relocation, family responsibilities and retirement can change a person's purposes, time horizons and ability to take risk. A plan made for one life stage may need different priorities later. Reviewing does not mean changing every goal whenever a headline appears; it means checking relevant evidence against the decision's assumptions.

For investments, a market value change can affect a plan without being a deposit or withdrawal. A $500 holding worth $450 has depreciated by $50; that record does not reveal whether it will recover. Keep contributions, withdrawals, fees and market changes distinct. A short-term bill should not rely on an assumed rebound.

A useful revision note follows actual event → present balance → remaining need and time → feasible change → review trigger. This is the second representation of the method; each part will appear in your final response.

Optional reference: FCAC's budget guidance recommends comparing a plan with actual income and spending and updating it as circumstances change. Read September 28, 2026. All required records and alternatives in this lesson are supplied.

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

The Magic of Compounding

You have read Ari’s saving record and the unexpected repair. Watch or read how interest can earn further interest. Then make an important distinction: this lesson’s Ari and Devon cases supply no interest. Their balances change through deposits and expenses.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a simple rising line and large text illustrate interest earned on earlier interest. The chart has no verified data source or forecast; returns can vary or be negative.

But what is it exactly? Basically, it's the snowball effect that happens with money and earning interest, or how interest makes money grow exponentially over time. If you put money into a savings account or investment that earns interest, in the beginning, interest is calculated on the initial amount you started with. But as that money starts to earn interest, you continue to earn interest not only that initial amount, but you begin to earn additional interest on the interest you've already made. And as the total amount of interest earned grows, the more interest you continue to earn. Hence, the snowball effect.

FINLIT 101 · The Magic of Compounding · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Can you use an assumed investment return to close Ari’s remaining gap?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Follow a complete example

Keep Ari's month-six deadline

Connect the video to this task. Separate the causes of change as you follow Ari’s revision: the repair reduced the balance; the future deposits rebuild it. No interest term belongs in this calculation.

After the repair, the balance is $170. The target gap is $350 − $170 = $180. With four deposits remaining, $180 ÷ 4 = $45 monthly is required.

The normal $30 amount would add only $120, ending at $290 and leaving $60 short. The supplied temporary budget change permits $45, so the revised plan can still meet the deadline. This conclusion relies on that confirmation; it does not assume every person can simply save more.

Complete revision: “The $80 repair leaves $170 after month two. To reach $350 at month six, Ari needs another $180 across four deposits, or $45 monthly. I would use the confirmed temporary adjustment for months 3–6 and check after month 3 that the first revised deposit happened and the $45 remains available. If it no longer fits, I would revisit a flexible date or target rather than erase the repair from the record.”

“Continue $25 and everything is fine” ignores the changed balance. “Start the original six-month plan again” changes the deadline without saying so. A complete revision preserves both the history and the condition being changed.

FINLIT activity · Try the original contribution comparison

From The Magic of Compounding Assignment, page 1. Question 3 compares $40 and $60 monthly over 40 years at an assumed 5% return, then changes contributions in stages. Questions 1–2 use a $300,000 target and retirement assumptions.

Try the first comparison as an optional calculator experiment: start at $0, use 40 years, an annual effective return of 5%, and 0% fees and inflation. Run $40 monthly, note the contributions and growth separately, then run $60. Our calculator deposits at month-end. The return is an illustration, not a prediction.

Return to Ari’s revision afterwards. Ari’s and Devon’s required tasks have no supplied interest, so use the actual balance and deposits only. Go to the practice fields.

The original opens in the course reader. Write in this lesson’s fields; buttons pictured in the original page are not active here.

Practise with support

Keep $30 monthly and move the date

Connect the video to this task. For the flexible-deadline practice, count the deposits required at $30 monthly. The compounding illustration cannot replace the missing contributions.

Use a changed version: Ari cannot make the temporary $45 adjustment, but the purchase deadline can now move. The balance after month two is still $170, the target is still $350, and $30 monthly is available from month three onward. No interest or additional resource is supplied.

Enter Deposits still needed and New completion month. Write My revised instruction, two sentences stating what changes and what stays. Use Check the revised date.

Six $30 deposits provide the remaining $180. They occur in months 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, so the new date is month 8. Feedback on month 6: six deposits are needed after month two, not from the beginning. Feedback on four deposits: four at $30 leave the plan $60 short. Feedback on six deposits of $45: that exceeds this changed version's available amount.

Compare your response with a model

Your current response

Model: “Keep the $350 target and actual $170 balance, but change the deadline from month 6 to month 8. Deposit $30 in each of months 3–8, and review after month 3 to confirm both the deposit and the new deadline remain workable.”


Optional budget-shock experiment


A separate fictional monthly budget has income $600, essentials $400, flexible spending $80, required debt payment $50 and saving $70. It initially balances. A one-time $60 repair creates a gap. Load this example into Test a budget change only if you want the additional experiment.


The case confirms that up to $60 of this month's flexible spending can be postponed without affecting essentials. Choose reduce flexible spending and enter $60 reduction. The revised flexible amount becomes $20, and the budget balances while keeping debt and saving allocations. Choose a review note such as “return to the ordinary budget next month if the repair does not recur.” Reducing saving is another possible adjustment, but its goal and recovery date must be reconsidered. New borrowing cannot be treated as free income; no loan approval or terms are supplied here.


The optional experiment is separate from Ari's balances. Do not move its $600 income into Ari's savings plan. Compare and revise your required practice instruction.

Apply independently

Protecting personal information · Lesson 2

Recognize scams and verify independently

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Watch or read Avoiding Scams: pause and verify; try the short case check
  5. Follow the video example or its written explanation
  6. Follow a complete example
  7. Practise with support
  8. Check your understanding
  9. Apply independently
  10. Review and complete
Optional reference · E-Transfer Fraud

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open E-Transfer Fraud ↗
Core vocabulary
Pretending to be another person or organization to gain trust.
A deceptive attempt to obtain information or access by posing as a trusted source.
Checking through a route obtained separately from the suspicious message.
A feature that raises a concern and calls for verification; it is not by itself a complete proof.

Start here

A familiar logo, a person's name or professional writing can make a message look convincing. The more useful question is what the sender wants you to do. A request to move money, reveal a code or install software deserves a pause even when the message looks polished.

You will classify several common fraud approaches, follow a bank-message and CRA-call example, practise choosing an independent verification route, and then prepare a response to a new job offer and a possibly genuine bank contact. Your product will identify the request, evidence, uncertainty and safe next step. The aim is careful verification, not assuming every unexpected contact is fraudulent.

Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause between the examples if useful. All required documents are supplied and answers save automatically. Guided work and six questions are practice; the final response plan and sign-offs form your evidence.

Vocabulary. Phishing is a deceptive contact designed to obtain information, money or access. Impersonation means pretending to be a trusted person or organization. A warning cue is a reason for concern, not complete proof of identity. Independent verification uses a route found separately from the questionable contact. A one-time code can authorize access or a transaction; it is not a harmless reference number.

Optional reference disclosure: Official scam and CRA guidance. The local dated records are sufficient. No student must open a website, call anyone, install software or send money.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Leah is a fictional adult reviewing an inbox. Leah has not clicked, replied, transferred money or shared a code. The following training cards show the whole relevant request; there are no hidden attachments to inspect.

Document A — Two contacts for the worked example

Contact Complete supplied wording and context
A: bank-looking text, October 6, 10:15 a.m. “Your money is at risk. Move your balance to our protected account within ten minutes. Reply with the sign-in code we just sent. Keep this investigation private.” It displays a bank name, but sender identity is not verified. Leah has a bank card and the previously installed bank app.
B: caller claiming to be CRA, October 6, 11:00 a.m. “I am Alex from a CRA processing office. We need to discuss a document supporting your return. I can provide my name, office location and callback number for you to verify.” No payment, password or code is requested in this supplied exchange. Leah filed a return, but has not verified this caller. Caller ID displays a government-style name.

Card B could be a genuine contact. That possibility does not authenticate it. Leah can end the call and independently verify before sharing information.

Document B — Five other requests to classify

All are fictional examples with unverified senders.

Card Supplied request
C: investment pitch “Guaranteed 20% return every week. Send $300 to the platform I chose today; there is no risk. Do not ask your bank because they will block your opportunity.”
D: job offer “We did not need an interview. Pay a $75 account-upgrade deposit to unlock your first paid online tasks. The balance on our screen proves your earnings.”
E: emergency claim “It's your cousin. My phone broke. Send $200 now to this new contact so I can get home. Please do not check with anyone else.”
F: purchase offer “Concert tickets at a very low price. Leave the marketplace payment system and transfer immediately to reserve them. I cannot show proof that I hold the tickets.”
G: relationship message A person Leah has only met online writes, “I care about you. Send $150 for my emergency trip to visit. If you trusted me, you would keep this between us.”

Document C — In-course source records

Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC), selected fraud descriptions and warnings; checked September 28, 2026: investment pitches may promise unrealistic guaranteed returns; job fraud may require payments to unlock work; emergency impersonation may demand urgent secret payments; merchandise fraud may use fake listings or payment claims; relationship fraud may build trust before requesting money. A scheme can combine types. The CAFC's current impersonation warning identifies “safe account” transfers and requests for codes or remote access as dangerous instructions; independently contact the actual institution.

CRA, “Verify it's the CRA calling,” checked September 28, 2026: CRA does call people. If uncertain, do not give personal information during the unverified call. Ask for the person's name, office and callback details, end the call, and use CRA's independently reached verification tool or official contact route. Caller ID is not proof. The tool does not include every direct employee number; an unrecognized result needs further official checking, not an automatic fraud verdict.

Read the documents

Which action in Card A creates the clearest immediate financial/access risk? Choose and select Check document reading.

Learn the method

Read the requested action first

A scam often tries to move a person from uncertainty to an irreversible action quickly. Identify the verb: send, transfer, install, reveal, deposit, approve. Then identify what could be lost: money, account access, personal information or control of a device. This is more reliable than judging a logo or spelling alone; convincing messages can be well written.

Pressure can be emotional as well as financial. A threat of closure, a promise of easy earnings, fear for a relative or a claim that love requires payment can all discourage checking. Recognizing the mechanism helps you pause without blaming the person receiving it. These approaches are designed to exploit ordinary hopes and responsibilities.

Classify by the story and the requested benefit

The label helps explain a pattern; it does not replace evidence. Card C offers investment returns, so investment fraud is the relevant pattern. Card D offers employment but asks the worker to pay, matching a job-fraud pattern. Card E impersonates a loved one in difficulty. Card F offers goods without adequate verification, matching a purchase/merchandise concern. Card G uses a developing relationship to seek funds.

Types can overlap. A supposed romantic partner who later recommends a guaranteed investment combines relationship and investment tactics. An online job that asks you to receive and forward money is different from ordinary paid work, even if it uses a real company's name. The CAFC advises verifying the actual employer independently and not paying deposits to unlock a job. A company existing does not prove that its name is being used by an authorized recruiter.

Break the sender's control over verification

Calling a number supplied only in the message keeps you inside the same contact's story. A separate route changes that. For a bank, use the number on a card or statement already held, or open the known bank app directly. For a family emergency, use the person's previously known number or another independently known contact. For an employer, find the real organization's official contact information independently and ask about the named vacancy and recruiter. Do not install an offered app or send money while checking.

For an investment, the source recommends independent research and registration checks with the provincial securities regulator or the national registration search. Registration is one check, not a guarantee of returns or proof that a message's sender is the registered person. This course does not ask you to evaluate or buy a real investment.

Keep the possibility of genuine contact open

CRA may need supporting tax information and may call. Therefore, “CRA never calls” is not a safe rule. Neither is “they knew my name, so I should answer everything.” The taught process lets a real request be handled through a verified route while denying an impersonator control of the interaction.

Asking for callback details collects a claim to check; it does not verify the claim. End the call before checking. Reach the CRA verification page independently. If its tool cannot verify a direct number, use the official CRA contact route for further checking. A result about a listed number also does not make caller ID impossible to spoof. The next conversation must use a route you have verified yourself.

Use a short decision record

Part Example from Card A
Request Transfer the balance and reveal a code.
Cues Time pressure, secrecy, “protected account” story, access code.
What is unknown Actual sender and whether there is a real bank issue.
Immediate boundary No transfer, code sharing or message link use.
Independent check Known bank app or contact details on the existing card.

The result of verification may be “request confirmed,” “fraud attempt confirmed,” or “still unresolved.” If unresolved, do not treat pressure as evidence. If exposure has already occurred, shift promptly to the response process in the next lesson rather than continuing the conversation.

Show a first-step hint

Optional hint: “In your response field, begin 'This contact asks for…'. Naming the action often makes the next step clearer.”

Watch or read · FINLIT 101

Avoiding Scams: pause and verify

Leah’s two contacts look different, but neither sender is verified. Watch or read the advice to slow down and double-check a request. In this lesson, “double-check” means reaching the organization through a separate, independently obtained route—not calling a number just because the message supplies it.

Read the video transcript

Visuals: a presenter speaks to the camera. Use the fictional message cards below to identify the claim, evidence and independent verification route.

First you'll want to keep a close eye on your inbox if you see a request for personal information Don't rush to respond. It's likely a scam You can always double check the sources legit with a phone call or just ignore it if you're unsure But be careful some scams can be very professional

FINLIT 101 · Avoiding Scams: pause and verify · selected excerpt, used with permission.

Which action independently checks the bank-looking request?

This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

Watch a worked decision

Pause, verify, then act

This demonstration includes a bank-looking message and a CRA web notice. The lesson record uses a bank-looking text and a caller claiming to be CRA. Follow the independent-verification method, then respond to the exact contact channel and request in the lesson cards.

Pause and decide: For the two fictional contacts, identify the requested action, one warning cue, and the verification route.

Read the narrated and visual transcript

Slide 1: Two messages, two requests

Read the action—not just the logo. A “Move your money to our safe account. Send the code.”; B “A new tax notice is available.”. What does each contact want you to do?

Two fictional contacts arrive. A bank-looking text says a transfer is at risk and asks the person to move money to a “safe account” and reply with a one-time code. A second notice says a tax message is waiting and tells the person to sign in through the usual government route. A familiar logo or official-sounding name does not identify the sender. Start by underlining the action each message requests and decide whether it is reversible or sensitive.

Slide 2: Spot pressure and sensitive requests

A cue raises concern; verify before acting. Urgency or threat; Transfer to a “safe” account; One-time code or password; Remote access or unusual payment. Cue ≠ proof • pause before an irreversible action.

Scams often create urgency, secrecy, threats, or an unexpected reward. Requests to transfer money to a “safe account,” buy gift cards, use cryptocurrency, install remote-access software, or share a password or one-time code are high-risk. Poor spelling can be a clue, but polished writing does not prove a message is real. A cue is evidence to slow down, not a complete identity test. Do not click, reply, transfer, or share secrets while pressured.

Slide 3: Verify through a separate route

Do not use the contact path supplied by the suspicious message. PAUSE; Find the official service independently; Ask if the request is real; Act only through a verified route. Known app • saved statement • official website typed independently

For a bank concern, open the known app or use contact details from a bank card or statement. Do not call a number included only in the unexpected text, and do not trust caller ID by itself. For a web notice, navigate to the known official site yourself rather than following a message link. If uncertain, talk to a trusted adult and ask the institution through an independently found route. A search result or advertisement may also be misleading; use the known official domain.

Slide 4: CRA contact needs a precise rule

CRA may contact people; caller ID is not proof. CRA may call, write, or send notifications; Caller ID can be spoofed; Never share passwords or security codes; Ask, end, verify independently if unsure. Use the CRA contact-verification tool or Canada.ca details.

Do not memorize the false rule “CRA never calls.” The Canada Revenue Agency may contact people by phone and other channels. A caller ID that displays a government name still does not prove who is calling. If a person is unsure, they can ask for the caller’s name, office, and callback number, end the call, and check using CRA’s official contact-verification tool or contact details found independently on Canada.ca. CRA may request some information for a legitimate identity check or missing tax information, but never share passwords or one-time security codes with an unexpected caller.

Slide 5: Pause: classify before you respond

Name the action, cue, and independent check. Message A: requested action?; Message B: safe route?; What remains uncertain?. Pause and write one sentence for each contact.

For the two fictional contacts, identify the requested action, one warning cue, and the verification route. Pause before choosing.

Slide 6: Worked answer: safe without guessing

Verify the contact; do not make an irreversible move. A Do not transfer or share the code; contact the bank independently.; B Navigate to Canada.ca yourself and check for the notice.; Unknown sender identity? Verify before acting.. Appearance is a clue—not authentication.

For message A, the safe-account transfer and code request are high-risk. Do not transfer or reply; contact the bank independently. For message B, the notification may be legitimate, but this fictional card is not proof. Navigate to Canada.ca yourself and check the account through the official route. If a caller claims to be CRA, remember that CRA can call, but caller ID can be spoofed. Ask for callback details, end the call, and verify independently if unsure. The lesson is neither “trust it” nor “all contacts are fake.” It is pause, verify, then act. If a learner already clicked or shared information, the response changes: stop interacting, secure the affected account from a trusted device, and promptly contact the relevant institution through an independently found route. Preserve the message and time, but do not reopen its link to collect evidence. If money was lost, contact local police promptly and report through current Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre guidance. Reporting does not guarantee recovery. A second person offering guaranteed reimbursement for an upfront fee is another reason to pause and verify.

Original CALM 10 classroom demonstration. Figures and people in this example are fictional; check current sources before real decisions.

Follow a complete example

For A, I ignore the polished appearance and read the request. Moving a balance to a stranger's “protected account” and sending a sign-in code could give away funds and access. The warning cues justify refusing those actions now. I can do that without first proving the sender's identity.

Connect the video to this task. Apply FINLIT’s pause-and-check advice separately to both contacts. A dangerous instruction and a potentially genuine call still require different explanations and independent checks.

For B, the request is different. CRA can seek supporting information, and the caller offers details for checking. That is compatible with a genuine call, but it remains an unverified claim. I use the official process before discussing personal tax information.

Complete response record:

A resembles bank-investigator impersonation: it requests a balance transfer and a sign-in code under time pressure and secrecy. Leah should not transfer, share the code, reply through the text or install anything. Open the known bank app or use the number on the existing bank card to ask whether the bank has a real concern. The source record supports that separate route; a logo does not authenticate this sender.

B may be genuine because CRA can call about tax documents. Leah should request the claimed name, office and callback details, say the contact will be checked, and end the call without sharing personal information. Reach CRA's verification page independently and use its official checking/contact route. If the number is not in the tool, obtain further official verification because direct employee numbers may be absent. Only continue the real matter through a verified channel; do not assume a caller-ID label or a polite tone proves authenticity.

“Block all government contact forever” would leave possible real business unresolved. “Send the code to show cooperation” would hand the unverified sender a sensitive tool. The plan protects access while keeping a route for legitimate service.

FINLIT activity · Turn warning signs into a verification plan

From Avoiding Frauds and Scams Assignment, page 1. Question 1 asks about action after CRA impersonation; question 2 asks about fraud and examples; question 3 asks for a list of 20 methods used by scammers.

Use the example-finding idea from questions 2–3 with the supplied contact cards. Name the request, point to a specific warning cue, and choose an independent verification route. A list of twenty is not required. For a CRA claim, use the current in-course CRA record: CRA can call, and an uncertain caller still needs checking.

Apply that process in the supported practice. Action after someone has shared information is taught in the next lesson. Go to the practice fields.

The original opens in the course reader. Write in this lesson’s fields; buttons pictured in the original page are not active here.

Practise with support

Keep Leah's A/B contacts. A second message from A says, “Install this remote-support app so we can secure your account.” No software has been installed. For B, this new fictional verification result is supplied: Leah independently reaches CRA using the official route; that service confirms a document request exists and explains a secure way to handle it. The original incoming caller's identity has not separately been established.

Connect the video to this task. When details change in practice, identify the exact request and available separate route again. CRA can call; an uncertain caller still needs verification.

Write three saved responses:

  1. What changed in A's request, and what boundary remains? Explain the added device-access risk.
  2. What did the independent check of B establish? Distinguish a confirmed matter and secure route from proof about the original caller.
  3. Write Leah's next action for each contact. Include a reason and avoid using the original contact's unverified route.
Show a first-step hint

“A now requests device access. B's official check confirms a task to handle securely, not every fact about who first called.”

Comparison feedback: “If you recommend installing the app to verify A, reverse that order: the risky access is what the contact wants. If you mark all of B fraudulent despite the supplied official result, update your conclusion. If you treat the original caller as verified, narrow what the new evidence actually establishes.”

Compare your response with a model

Your current response

Matching model:


    

  1. “A adds a request for remote access, which could expose the device or accounts. Leah still should not install, share codes or move money.”
    2. 

  2. “The independently reached CRA service confirmed a real document request and a secure route. It did not establish the identity of the original incoming caller.”

  3. “For A, contact the bank using the existing app/card route and preserve the messages safely. For B, use the secure route provided during the independently verified CRA interaction to address the actual document request; do not send information back through the original unverified contact.”

Check your understanding

Apply independently

Devon is a fictional adult. Prepare one two-contact verification plan. Neither contact has been acted on.


Document D — Unrequested job message, October 12. “I recruit for Summit Parcel, a real-looking company name. You are approved for remote order-checking work. Deposit $90 to unlock the work dashboard today; then receive customer payments in your personal account and forward them to our operator. Use only our chat, because the public office does not handle this program.” Devon did not apply and has no verified recruiter contact. No actual address, link or payment information is supplied.

You can end this call and check it through your usual bank channel.” The caller gives a proposed time and asks for no password, code, payment, software installation or personal document in this exchange. articles.fl4-05:
Protecting personal information · Lesson 5

Coordinate a recovery plan

How to complete this lesson
  1. Start here
  2. Meet the situation and read the documents
  3. Learn the method
  4. Follow a complete example
  5. Practise with support
  6. Check your understanding
  7. Apply independently
  8. Review and complete
Optional reference · Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA

All facts needed for the activities are supplied in the lesson. Use the named original for further reading or to check current details.

Open Report a Scam or Identity Theft — CRA ↗
Core vocabulary
An ordered response to an incident that addresses security, evidence and appropriate reporting.
The organization controlling the account or service involved.
A notice asking potential creditors to take additional identity-verification steps.
A record separating planned actions, actions taken and confirmed results.

Start here

After fraud, a person may need several kinds of help. A bank can address a payment route; an email provider can address account access; police and fraud-reporting services have reporting roles. Sending one report does not automatically complete the other jobs. A calm plan assigns each action to the organization that can carry it out and records what has actually happened.

You will coordinate a response to a ticket-payment and password incident, update the plan when providers reply, and then build a distinct plan for identity information and an independently observed tax-account change. The final product is a prioritized response plan with specific recipients, safe routes, evidence and follow-up conditions.

Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Learn the method → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Work in small parts and pause after the response table if useful. Everything happens in the fictional record. Do not open a real financial account, disclose a SIN, contact an agency or ask another person to supervise. Guided work and six questions are practice; the new independent plan and sign-offs complete this lesson. Your writing saves automatically.

Vocabulary. Recovery is the process of responding to an incident and restoring security or addressing losses; it does not promise that money will be returned. An affected provider controls a relevant account or service. Identity fraud involves misuse of identity information; exposure and confirmed misuse should be distinguished. A credit report records credit information; a fraud alert asks potential creditors to take additional identity-verification steps. A recovery scam offers to recover losses as a way to demand more money, access or secrets. A status log separates planned actions, actions taken and confirmed results.

Optional disclosure: Official recovery records and routes. The in-course records below support all required decisions. Live pages are optional for current real use.

Meet the situation and read the documents

Ari is a fictional adult who tried to purchase a concert ticket. The incident has two confirmed exposures: a personally approved payment induced by deception, and a password entered on a false delivery page. Read the complete starting record before choosing agencies.

Document A — Incident log, October 18, 2026

Time / category Supplied facts
2:00 p.m., payment Ari personally approved a $160 electronic transfer from Ari's bank to a supposed ticket seller. The transfer shows as deposited in the genuine bank app. No ticket was supplied. The actual recipient/account details are omitted from this course.
2:10 p.m., information entry A false “ticket delivery registration” page asked for email login details. Ari entered the email login/password, name and mailing address. That same password is used for a music account. The email is the music account's recovery address.
Not entered / not observed No SIN, date of birth, identity-document image, banking password, payment-card details or one-time code was entered. No app was installed and no remote access granted. No new credit account, unfamiliar bank transaction or CRA-account change is reported.
2:20 p.m., current status Ari can still access the bank, email and music services through previously known routes. A separate updated personal device is available. No provider has yet been contacted and no security change has been recorded.
Evidence already available Seller conversation, original transfer record, message requesting the delivery login and a screenshot without the entered password. No need to reopen the false page.

Document B — Available independent routes and controls

  • Ari's genuine bank app, opened directly on the separate device, contains the bank's fraud-contact route. The bank can review the transfer and advise on the payment/account response. The record does not promise the deposited transfer can be recovered.
  • Ari has the known email app and a saved official music-service bookmark. These fictional providers allow a unique new password, recovery-detail review, review/sign-out of other sessions and MFA. Their guide says a password change does not automatically end all other sessions. Official recovery support is available if access is lost. These interface details are case assumptions, not universal service instructions.
  • The official local police website and CAFC's official “What to do if you're a victim of fraud” page can be reached independently. The latter links to Report Cybercrime and Fraud, the official online reporting route. A course response is not sent to either service.

Document C — New message from an unverified stranger, 2:25 p.m.

I recover stolen ticket money. I know your loss was $160. Pay my $40 administration fee and send your email verification code, and I guarantee the money will be returned today. Do not speak to the bank because that will delay us.

The sender is not independently verified. No actual address, link, telephone number or code is supplied. Knowing the amount does not explain how the sender obtained it or establish authority.

Document D — In-course agency and response records

CAFC, “What to do if you're a victim of fraud,” and “Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre Impersonation”; checked September 28, 2026. Keep relevant records, promptly contact the institution that transferred money, and report fraud to local police and the official fraud/cybercrime reporting route. Recovery offers can demand fees or more information. Independently reach official services; a convincing name, document or detail from the incident is not sufficient verification. Reporting does not guarantee recovery.

Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, “Protecting yourself from identity theft online”; checked September 28, 2026. Identify the information and accounts affected, secure compromised/reused credentials and connected accounts, contact affected providers and monitor relevant activity. Choose identity-protection measures from the actual exposure or misuse, not an invented list of every possible stolen document.

CRA, “Report a scam or identity theft”; checked September 28, 2026. Suspected CRA-account compromise or unauthorized changes to CRA information, including bank or address details, warrant contacting CRA through its official reporting/support route. An unfamiliar call is not itself proof of an account change. A person can independently open the official CRA page to identify the relevant secure or telephone option. CRA account support is distinct from a CAFC report.

Service Canada, “SIN fraud and data breaches”; checked September 28, 2026; page modified May 13, 2026. Suspected SIN misuse or exposure calls for monitoring credit information and relevant accounts. The page points to both Canadian credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion, and explains fraud alerts and responses when fraud is identified. It says a person does not need to notify the SIN Program about suspected misuse or a breach. Issuing a new SIN is not a routine cure: the old number and its records do not simply disappear. Contact affected institutions or government programs for the misuse involving them.

Read the documents

Which action best fits Ari's confirmed financial event? Choose and select Check document reading.

Learn the method

Start with an exposure map

List what actually left the person's control: money, a password, card details, a SIN, an identity document or device access. Then connect each item to its provider. This is more useful than a universal instruction to “call everyone.” Ari's payment belongs in a bank response; the reused credential belongs in email and music-account responses.

Separate facts from possible consequences. Ari's name and address could assist future impersonation, so continued caution matters. Those facts do not establish a new credit account or tax-account intrusion. Conversely, if a case supplies a SIN exposure and an independently observed unauthorized tax-account change, identity and CRA responses have concrete reasons. Match the measure to the evidence.

Prioritize time-sensitive controls, then coordinate

Do not postpone urgent provider contact while perfecting an evidence file. Ari already has the essential payment record and message. The bank needs prompt notice of the deceptive transfer, and exposed accounts need prompt protection through independent trusted routes. Write an order and a reason; some actions could occur close together rather than waiting days for one organization to finish.

For the connected credentials, securing the recovery email before the music account is defensible because access to that email can help reset the music account. Follow the supplied session and recovery controls as well as changing passwords. A person who has lost access may need the provider's official recovery process instead. The course cannot certify that a real account is secure.

Deceptive transfer or exposed financial account Financial institution through an existing statement/card or genuine app Payment details and truthful account of approval/exposure; ask about protection, investigation and possible recovery.
Entered/reused credentials Affected account providers through known apps or independently reached official support Affected account names and access status; secure credentials, sessions and recovery methods.
Fraud incident or identity misuse Local police via independently reached official local route; CAFC-linked Report Cybercrime and Fraud Dated incident, amounts/categories, evidence and provider references; reporting is separate from account controls.
Unauthorized CRA-account information change CRA through the official Canada.ca report-scam/identity-theft page Identify the observed change and request the relevant account protection/identity assistance.
SIN exposure or credit identity concerns Both credit bureaus through links on Service Canada's official SIN page, plus affected creditors/programs when relevant Review reports, ask about appropriate alerts or dispute unfamiliar credit activity; an alert is not a universal account lock.

The table supplies routes rather than memorized phone numbers. A route is independent when it comes from a trusted source already held or an official page reached without the suspicious message's link. A caller who says “use this number to verify me” is still controlling the proposed route. An official-looking logo or knowledge of an incident does not change that.

Keep a living status log

Use three columns: action planned → action taken and reference → result or next check. “Reported to bank” does not mean “money refunded.” “Changed password” does not mean every active session ended. “Subscription closed” does not mean a disputed charge was reversed. Specific status language prevents false reassurance and shows which task remains.

Record times, amounts, contact labels, categories disclosed, responses and case references. Do not put a password, SIN, full account number or one-time code into the course. Existing evidence can be kept safely; do not revisit an unsafe page or continue a scam conversation to gather more. Real institutions may have secure evidence processes; reach them independently before sharing sensitive originals.

Reject a second loss without blame

An offer of guaranteed recovery can be attractive after a loss. That is why a recovery scam may repeat the amount, impersonate an agency and insist on a fee, code or secrecy. Ari's stranger asks for both money and an email code while discouraging the bank. Stop that interaction and preserve the existing message. The person's first mistake does not create an obligation to keep paying or to prove they deserve help.

Optional first-step hint: “Draw two branches from Ari's record: $160 → bank; reused email/music password → connected providers. Add reporting and follow-up after those controls.”

Follow a complete example

I begin with the financial fact: Ari approved the transfer under deceptive circumstances. I do not call it an unapproved transaction, and I do not assume a deposited transfer can simply be cancelled. I direct prompt notice to the bank through its genuine app, using the separate device.

Next I connect the email and music accounts. Both use the entered password, and the email is a recovery path for music. The provider guide tells me to handle sessions separately. The stranger's knowledge of $160 does not verify the offer; the proposed $40 payment and email code would create further exposure.

Stop using the false delivery page and do not answer the recovery stranger, pay $40 or send a code. Promptly secure the email account, then music, through the known app/bookmark. The unsupported shortcut is “CAFC will recover everything; wait for its answer.” It leaves the bank and exposed credentials unattended and invents a result. Coordination means several specific jobs, each with a relevant recipient.
